title: tidypredict_fit() disagrees with predict() for aorsf regression forests
description:
For an `aorsf` regression forest, the expression from `tidypredict_fit()` does not reproduce the model's own `predict()`. The two are highly correlated but differ well beyond rounding: 254 of 2930 rows differ by more than 0.01 on an outcome that spans 4.11 to 5.88.

```r
library(aorsf)
set.seed(123)

d <- modeldata::ames[, c("Sale_Price", "Lot_Area", "Gr_Liv_Area", "Year_Built", "Full_Bath")]
d$Sale_Price <- log10(d$Sale_Price)

m <- orsf(d, Sale_Price ~ ., n_tree = 20)

own <- predict(m, new_data = d)[, 1]
tp  <- tidypredict::tidypredict_to_column(d, m)$fit

max(abs(own - tp))
#> [1] 0.04904059
cor(own, tp)
#> [1] 0.9994998
sum(abs(own - tp) > 0.01)
#> [1] 254

head(own, 3)
#> [1] 5.24747 5.06462 5.20802
head(tp, 3)
#> [1] 5.25207 5.07145 5.21183
```

The pattern (very high correlation, small but structural per-row differences) looks like a difference in how the per-tree predictions are combined rather than a mistranslated split. `tidypredict_fit()` reads slightly high on the rows I inspected.

`aorsf` 0.1.6, `tidypredict` 1.1.1.9000.

Context: this surfaced while surveying backends for orbital support. aorsf is currently blocked on this, since orbital cannot be more correct than the expression it consumes.

title: Expose the class rule for decision-value and calibrated-probability models
description:
`tidypredict_output_type()` tells a consumer *what shape* a classification model's fit returns, which is enough to know whether to cut at 0 or at 0.5. It is not enough to know **which class a value on either side of that cut means**, or **where the cut actually is**. Two backends need each, and both currently force a consumer to reach into the fitted object.

### 1. Decision orientation (LiblineaR)

`tidypredict_output_type()` returns `"decision"`, so a consumer knows to cut at 0. But LiblineaR orients its decision function toward `ClassNames[1]`, the model's own class order, which is independent of the order of the outcome's factor levels:

```r
library(parsnip)
d <- iris[iris$Species != "setosa", ]

for (ord in list(c("versicolor", "virginica"), c("virginica", "versicolor"))) {
  d$Species <- factor(as.character(d$Species), levels = ord)
  f <- fit(svm_linear(mode = "classification", engine = "LiblineaR"), Species ~ ., d)
  cat("levels:", levels(d$Species),
      "| ClassNames:", as.character(f$fit$ClassNames),
      "| tidypredict_outcome_levels:", tidypredict::tidypredict_outcome_levels(f$fit), "\n")
}
#> levels: versicolor virginica | ClassNames: versicolor virginica | tidypredict_outcome_levels: versicolor virginica
#> levels: virginica versicolor | ClassNames: versicolor virginica | tidypredict_outcome_levels: virginica versicolor
```

`tidypredict_outcome_levels()` follows the factor levels, so it does not carry the orientation. Assuming "positive means the second level" inverts **every** class prediction whenever the two orders differ (measured agreement 0.00).

### 2. Where the cut is (kernlab)

`ksvm()` reports `"prob"`, and the probabilities from `tidypredict_fit()` are exact (7.8e-16 against `predict()`). But kernlab assigns a class by the sign of the decision function while calibrating the probabilities separately with Platt scaling, so the class rule is not "larger probability wins". The two cross at `1 / (1 + exp(B))`:

```r
f <- fit(svm_linear(mode = "classification", engine = "kernlab"), Species ~ ., d)
B <- f@fit@prob.model[[1]]$B
# cut at 0.5              -> 0.98 agreement with predict()
# cut at 1 / (1 + exp(B)) -> 1.00
```

A consumer that cuts at 0.5 is systematically wrong for rows near the boundary, not merely imprecise.

### Suggestion

Something along the lines of a `tidypredict_class_rule()` returning the threshold and the level a value above it means, so that both cases are answerable from the tidypredict API rather than from package internals. The exact shape is yours to pick; the ask is that the orientation and the threshold be reachable at all.

For context: orbital hit both of these adding SVM support (tidymodels/orbital#164) and currently works around them by reading `ClassNames` and `@prob.model` off the fit, which is the coupling this would remove.

title: CRAN reverse dependency check: XGBoost DART/dropout models no longer detected by booster name
description:
Upstream XGBoost tracking issue: https://github.com/dmlc/xgboost/issues/12260

Hi, I am looking at XGBoost CRAN reverse dependency failures for XGBoost 3.4.0-dev, and `tidypredict` is failing on DART/dropout model tests.

XGBoost now deprecates `booster = "dart"` as a separate booster name and canonicalizes it to `gbtree`, while preserving dropout behavior and saving `weight_drop` in model JSON for models trained with dropout parameters such as `rate_drop`, `skip_drop`, or `one_drop`.

The current `get_xgb_json_params()` logic appears to infer DART by searching saved JSON for `"name":"dart"`, and only extracts `weight_drop` when that string is present. With current XGBoost, the saved JSON has `"name":"gbtree"` and includes `weight_drop`, so `weight_drop` is not extracted and the generated formulas can diverge from native `predict()`.

The revdep failures include:

- `DART booster with rate_drop > 0 predictions match native predict`
- `DART booster weight_drop is extracted correctly`

Suggested fix: detect dropout models from the presence of `weight_drop`, not from the serialized booster name, and extract/apply `weight_drop` whenever it is present.

Thanks.

title: tidypredict_test() for xgboost misses over-prediction (missing abs() on fit_diff)
description:
`xgb_booster()`, the helper behind `tidypredict_test.xgb.Booster()`, compares predictions without taking the absolute value, so it only detects differences in one direction.

https://github.com/tidymodels/tidypredict/blob/main/R/tidypredict_test.R#L511-L512

```r
raw_results$fit_diff <- raw_results$base - raw_results$fit_te
raw_results$fit_threshold <- raw_results$fit_diff > threshold
```

Every other method in the file takes the absolute value: `tidypredict_test_default()` (L302), `tidypredict_test.glmnet()` (L403), `lgb_booster()` (L616), and `catboost_model()` (L759) all use `abs(...) > threshold`. The xgboost path is the only one that doesn't, which looks unintentional rather than deliberate.

The effect is that when `tidypredict_fit()` over-predicts relative to native `predict()`, `fit_diff` is negative, never exceeds `threshold`, and `$alert` stays `FALSE`.

## Reproducible example

Starting from a model that legitimately passes, I inflated `base_score` in the parsed model so the generated formula over-predicts by about 1.48 on every row:

```r
library(tidypredict)
library(xgboost)

d <- xgb.DMatrix(as.matrix(mtcars[, -9]), label = mtcars$am)
m <- xgb.train(
  params = list(max_depth = 2, objective = "reg:squarederror", base_score = 0.5),
  data = d, nrounds = 4, verbose = 0
)

# Sabotage: base_score of 1.5 instead of the true 0.5
pm <- parse_model(m)
pm$general$params$base_score <- 1.5

base <- predict(m, d)
te <- rlang::eval_tidy(tidypredict_fit(pm), mtcars)

max(abs(base - te))              #> 1.482051
sum((base - te) > 1e-7)          #> 0   <- rule used by xgb_booster()
sum(abs(base - te) > 1e-7)       #> 32  <- rule used everywhere else
```

A whole-model error of 1.48 on all 32 rows goes completely undetected.

## Impact

Roughly 20 tests in `tests/testthat/test-model-xgboost.R` assert `expect_false(result$alert)` through this path, covering every supported objective, DART, stump trees, deep trees, and the custom `base_score` cases. All of them currently verify only one direction of error.

The reported max difference has the same issue and can print a negative number:

https://github.com/tidymodels/tidypredict/blob/main/R/tidypredict_test.R#L527

```r
difference <- data.frame(fit_diff = max(raw_results$fit_diff))
```

## Suggested fix

Wrap both in `abs()` to match the other methods:

```r
raw_results$fit_diff <- abs(raw_results$base - raw_results$fit_te)
raw_results$fit_threshold <- raw_results$fit_diff > threshold
```

Worth expecting a few currently-passing xgboost tests to start failing once the other direction is actually checked, in which case the per-objective thresholds may need revisiting (they already range from `1e-7` to `1e-5`).

Found while comparing tidypredict's xgboost handling against the ONNX-based path in [orbital](https://github.com/posit-dev/orbital).

title: Metadata and infrastructure upkeep
description:
- [ ] **`Depends: R (>= 3.6)` is wrong.** The package uses R 4.1+ syntax: backslash lambdas at `R/model-h2o.R:175`, `R/model-multinom.R:34`, `R/tree-nested.R:236`, plus a native pipe. On R 3.6 it would not even parse. Set `R (>= 4.1)`, which also matches the project's own stated floor; tidyverse's five-releases-back rule currently puts it around 4.2.
- [ ] **DESCRIPTION `Description` model list is stale**: no mention of `glmnet`, `LiblineaR`, `ObliqueForest` (aorsf), `blackboost` (mboost), `multinom`, `rq`/`rqs` (quantreg), the three H2O classes, `lda_shrink_mean`/`lda_shrink_cov`/`lda_emp_bayes_eigen`, or the `mixo_spls`/`mixo_plsda`/`mixo_splsda` variants. Also `xgb.Booster.complete()` is not a model class — the method is on `xgb.Booster`. Rather than enumerating 40 classes, consider a short prose sentence plus a pointer to the pkgdown model list.
- [ ] `Suggests` is not in case-insensitive alphabetical order: `mda` precedes `mboost`, `methods` sits after `mixOmics`, and `rmarkdown`/`RSQLite` sit after `sparsediscrim`. `usethis::use_tidy_description()` fixes this.
- [ ] **Unused Suggests**: `methods` and `mlbench` have zero references anywhere in `R/`, `tests/` or `vignettes/`. (`covr` is also unreferenced but is conventionally kept for the coverage workflow.) No `Imports` package is unused.
- [ ] `catboost` is used in tests and `vignettes/catboost.Rmd` but is not in `Suggests`, since it is not on CRAN. Calls are guarded by `skip_if_not_installed()`, so check stays clean, but an `Additional_repositories:` entry or a comment would tell contributors how to install it.
- [ ] **`Authors@R`** has no ORCIDs and no copyright-holder/funder entry. Tidymodels convention includes `person("Posit Software, PBC", role = c("cph", "fnd"), comment = c(ROR = "03wc8by49"))`. Note the mismatch with `LICENSE`, which names "tidypredict authors" as copyright holder while no `cph` role exists in `Authors@R`; `YEAR: 2021` is also stale for a package under active development.
- [ ] **`NEWS.md:3-90` bullets are not ordered per the project convention** (non-function bullets first, then alphabetical by function name); `tidypredict_fit()` bullets appear at lines 5, 7, 9, 11, 21 and 88, interleaved with "Added support for …" bullets at 3, 13, 15, … Also, nearly every dev bullet cites `(#232)` as a catch-all; attribute them to their real issues where those exist. Prose nits: `:3` "Regression predictions average the individual trees" (you average predictions, not trees); `:19` British "honours" → "honors"; `:340` doubled "with"; `:314` "Cubst" (the last two pre-existing).
- [ ] **`.github/workflows/pr-commands.yaml:17`** uses `actions/checkout@v3` while every other workflow uses `@v4`, and it lacks the `permissions:` block that `R-CMD-check.yaml`, `pkgdown.yaml` and `test-coverage.yaml` all have. **`.github/workflows/lock.yaml:11`** pins `dessant/lock-threads@v2`, several major versions behind (v5 is current), by tag rather than SHA. `usethis::use_tidy_github_actions()` refreshes both.
- [ ] **`cran-comments.md` and `revdep/` are stale.** `cran-comments.md` claims "0 errors | 0 warnings | 0 notes" and "3 reverse dependencies, 0 new problems", consistent with `revdep/cran.md`, but `revdep/README.md` records the run against `tidypredict 1.0.1` → `1.0.1.9000` on 2026-02-26 while DESCRIPTION is now `1.1.0.9000`. The revdep results predate the entire dev cycle documented in NEWS (~25 new model families). Re-run `revdepcheck::revdep_check()` and regenerate before submission. `revdep/data.sqlite` should probably be gitignored.
- [ ] `.Rbuildignore` is complete for everything relevant, but has two dead entries worth pruning: `^CRAN-RELEASE$` (superseded by `CRAN-SUBMISSION`) and `travis.yml`. `README.Rmd` and `model.csv` are unanchored regexes; `^README\.Rmd$` is the convention.
- [ ] `.gitignore` ignores `pkgdown` and `docs`, yet an untracked `pkgdown/` directory exists in the working tree (`git ls-files pkgdown` returns nothing). If it holds intentional customization — extra CSS, favicons — it is silently untracked and will be lost. Worth verifying.
- [ ] `codecov.yml` sets `informational: true` on both project and patch with a 1% threshold, so coverage never blocks a PR. Given that `R/model-ranger.R` reads as 21.17% against 92.91% overall without anyone noticing, consider a non-informational patch target.
- [ ] No `Config/usethis/last-upkeep` field; `usethis::use_tidy_upkeep_issue()` would surface this kind of staleness on a schedule.
- [ ] `R/model-earth.R` uses the magrittr `%>%` throughout (22 occurrences) against the project's base-pipe convention, and `importFrom(dplyr, "%>%")` at `R/tidypredict-package.R:19` exists only for it. Converting the chain to `|>` lets the import go. Also `gsub(.x$column, "", .x$term)` at `:63` treats a column name as a regex. `<<-` is used at `R/model-lightgbm.R:69,142`, `R/model-bart.R:34`, `R/model-C5.0.R:77`.
- [ ] `identical(tidypredict_fit(model), tidypredict_fit(parse_model(model)))` is `FALSE` for randomForest and ranger. The values agree exactly; the expressions differ only in leaf numeric attributes, because `tidypredict_fit.randomForest` and `parse_model.randomForest` use two separate builders. rpart, partykit, cforest and aorsf are `identical`. Unifying the builders would stop the two paths drifting.

title: bart: a zero-variance predictor is rejected with an unhelpful message
description:
Found by the degenerate-fits battery. Lower priority than #362; filing so it is written down.

A `dbarts` fit containing a zero-variance predictor is rejected:

```r
set.seed(1)
d <- data.frame(x1 = rnorm(120), xconst = 1)
d$y <- 2 * d$x1 + rnorm(120, sd = 0.3)

m <- dbarts::bart2(y ~ x1 + xconst, data = d, n.trees = 5, n.samples = 5,
                   n.burn = 5, keepTrees = TRUE, verbose = FALSE)
tidypredict_fit(m)
#> Error: Unable to map the predictors of the `dbarts::bart()` model onto the
#>   columns of the data.
```

`predict()` works on the same model, so the fit itself is fine; dbarts simply never splits on a constant column, and the mapping from stored predictors back to data columns does not survive that.

This is at least an honest abort rather than a wrong number, and a constant predictor is an unusual thing to hand a model, so it may be reasonable to leave. But the message tells the user nothing about which predictor caused it or why, and the same shape passes for every other supported model except `randomForest` (#362) and `aorsf`, which refuses to fit at all.

If it is worth fixing, naming the offending column in the error would be a cheap improvement even without supporting the case.

title: `helper-h2o.R` emits 11 warnings instead of skipping cleanly
description:
`devtools::test()` currently reports `WARN 11`, all from `skip_if_no_h2o()` (`test-h2o.R:2,19,37,55,74,88,103,119,136` and `test-tidymodels.R:89,118`):

```
Your H2O cluster version is (2 years, 7 months and 15 days) old. There may be a newer version available.
```

`tests/testthat/helper-h2o.R:3-17` calls `h2o::h2o.init()` at `:8`, which either starts a JVM or silently attaches to whatever is listening on localhost:54321. The wrapper uses `suppressMessages()` plus `tryCatch(error =)`, but `h2o.init()` reports a version mismatch as a **warning**, which neither suppresses nor catches — so it surfaces as a testthat warning rather than a clean skip. It also treats a stale foreign cluster as success, and never shuts the JVM down.

**Fix.**

- `skip_on_cran()`, and `skip()` early when `Sys.which("java") == ""`.
- Probe with `h2o.clusterIsUp()` / `h2o.connect()` before falling back to `h2o.init()`.
- Wrap the probe in `withCallingHandlers(..., warning = function(w) invokeRestart("muffleWarning"))` plus `capture.output()`, and treat a version-mismatch warning as a skip condition rather than success.
- Memoize the result so the cluster starts at most once.
- Register `withr::defer(h2o::h2o.shutdown(prompt = FALSE), testthat::teardown_env())`.

While here: `tidypredict_test.H2OMultinomialModel` errors for non-syntactic class labels. `R/model-h2o.R:177` does `preds[, domain, drop = FALSE]`, but H2O prefixes probability column names with `p` when a domain level is not a syntactic name — `y = factor(mtcars$cyl)` gives `domain = c("4","6","8")` while `names(h2o.predict(...))` is `c("predict","p4","p6","p8")`, so it fails with "undefined columns selected". The **fitted formula itself is correct**; only the test helper breaks, and it is uncovered because the suite uses `iris`. Fix: index positionally with `as.matrix(preds[, -1, drop = FALSE])`, which is the assumption `tidypredict_test.H2OBinomialModel` already makes at `:153`.

`CONTRIBUTING.md` would also benefit from a note on the h2o and catboost local-setup requirements, since a new contributor running `devtools::test()` today just sees 11 opaque warnings.

title: Tests record verdicts instead of asserting them
description:
This is the reason a recent audit found 27 confirmed silent-wrong-prediction bugs against a clean `R CMD check` and 1770 passing tests, so it is worth treating as a first-class issue rather than a cleanup.

**The dominant test idiom does not assert correctness.** `expect_snapshot(tidypredict_test(model))` *records* the verdict. If a regression flips "All results are within the difference threshold" into an alert, that is an acceptable-looking snapshot diff, not a failure. The second most common idiom, `expect_identical(tidypredict_fit(model), tidypredict_fit(parse_model(model)))`, is a serialization round-trip: it proves the two paths agree with each other, not that either agrees with the model.

Files whose only correctness evidence is a snapshot:

| file                   | evidence                                                                                      |
|------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `test-model-glm.R`     | 9 snapshots, **zero** `predict()` calls (lines 39-104)                                        |
| `test-model-xgboost.R` | 1521 lines, 48 `tidypredict_test()` calls, **3** `predict()` calls (`:747`, `:1371`, `:1382`) |
| `test-model-ranger.R`  | a single `predict()` comparison at `:47` covering 9 snapshots                                 |
| `test-model-rf.R`      | 5 `predict()` calls in 301 lines                                                              |
| `test-model-glmnet.R`  | 5 `predict()` calls in 428 lines; family and multinomial coverage is snapshot-only            |

`test-model-catboost.R` is the counter-example to copy: it calls `catboost.predict()` extensively from `:531`.

**Proposed change.** Every model test should include at least one assertion of the form

```r
expect_equal(
  rlang::eval_tidy(tidypredict_fit(model), df),
  unname(predict(model, df)),
  tolerance = 1e-12
)
```

with the tolerance loosened only where the engine genuinely computes in float32 (and a comment saying so). Where a snapshot is kept for its message, pair it with `expect_false(result$alert)` — `test-h2o.R:15,33` already does this.

**A second pattern worth fixing at the same time: the tests systematically exercise only the configuration that happens to work.** This is not one file's oversight, it recurs:

- every categorical catboost test uses exactly 3 factor levels, and 3 is essentially the only count that works;
- every ksvm test uses 2 numeric predictors, and the scaling bug needs exactly 1;
- every LightGBM NA test trains *with* NA present, the one `missing_type` where the routing is correct;
- the bart tests use `ntree = 1..10` where the dbarts default is 200;
- no rf/ranger test uses a factor predictor, which is where both are badly broken.

Adding these specific configurations would have caught most of the audit's findings.

Smaller related items:

- `test-model-glm.R:25` and `test-model-earth.R:21` mutate `model$coefficients <- round(..., 7)` before comparing, so both sides derive from the same mutated object. Label these "round trip" so they are not mistaken for correctness tests.
- Zero uses of `withr::local_seed()`; ~250 global `set.seed()` calls leak RNG state into later tests (`test-model-rf.R` reseeds 17 times). One genuinely unseeded random fit at `test-model-nnet.R:212`.
- `tests/testthat/helper-printing.R` `round_print()` has no callers and is fragile: `:10-12` passes a captured number to `sub()` as an unanchored regex, so `.` matches any character and a shorter number matches inside a longer one, and the pattern `[0-9]+\.?[0-9]+` never matches single-digit or `1e-05` values. Delete it or fix and use it.
- Backwards-compat fixtures: the v3 set is well designed (`pm` + `newdata` + `expected`, with `expected` from the modelling package's own `predict()`), but no fixture records the producing package or R version; `generate-v3-fixtures.R:26` uses one `set.seed(123)` for five sequential fits, so reordering silently changes the rf/xgb fixtures; there is no generator for `cubist-v2-regression.rds` at all; the v2 fixtures store no `expected` (structure only); and `test-backwards-compat-v3.R:9` uses `tolerance = 1e-6` where the suite standard is `1e-12`.
- Bare `tempfile()` instead of `withr::local_tempfile()` at `test-model-earth.R:24`, `test-model-glm.R:28`, `test-model-lm.R:29`, `test-model-glmnet.R:23,198`, `test-model-nullmodel.R:66,75`.

title: Tests fail rather than skip without several Suggests packages
description:
The suite makes 693 `skip_if_not_installed()` calls overall, so discipline is broadly good, but these files would **fail** rather than skip on a machine lacking the relevant Suggests package:

- `test-model-earth.R` — no skips at all; `earth::earth()` at `:2`, `yaml::` at `:25`
- `test-model-rpart.R` — no skips; `rpart::rpart()` from `:2`
- `test-model-ranger.R` — only `skip_on_cran()`/`skip_on_os()` at `:2-4`, no `skip_if_not_installed("ranger")`
- `test-model-glmnet.R` — skips only `survival` at `:140`; glmnet, parsnip, dbplyr and yaml unguarded
- `test-model-rf.R:4` — randomForest used from `:4` but skipped only at `:274`/`:294`
- `test-model-glm.R:29` and `test-model-lm.R:29` — `yaml::write_yaml()` unguarded (contrast `test-model-nullmodel.R:61`, which does skip)
- `test-sql.R:3` — `dbplyr::simulate_dbi()` at file top
- `test-tidymodels.R:1-9` — `earth::etitanic` plus parsnip, no skip

**Fix.** Add the corresponding `skip_if_not_installed()` calls.

**Also worth adding, and probably the highest-value CI change available here:** one workflow job that installs **only** hard dependencies and runs the suite. With ~45 Suggests, none of them required, that is the only way this class of problem gets caught automatically.

Separately, `test-model-nullmodel.R:34,48` use `parsnip:::predict.nullmodel`. A triple colon into another package's internals draws an `R CMD check` note in some configurations and will break silently if parsnip renames the method — call `predict()` and let dispatch find it.

title: ranger tests run on macOS only
description:
23 of the 28 `test_that()` blocks in `tests/testthat/test-model-ranger.R` carry `skip_on_cran()` **plus** `skip_on_os("windows")` **plus** `skip_on_os("linux")`. No other test file in the suite uses `skip_on_os` (grep: ranger 46, xrf 1).

Consequences:

- Against the CI matrix in `.github/workflows/R-CMD-check.yaml` (macos-latest, windows-latest, ubuntu-latest × devel/release/oldrel-1), the 374-line ranger parser is exercised on **1 of 5 jobs**, and never on CRAN.
- `.github/workflows/test-coverage.yaml` runs on ubuntu-latest, so Codecov reports `R/model-ranger.R` at **21.17%** against 92.91% overall. That figure is a measurement artifact: forcing `NOT_CRAN="true"` locally gives **222/222 lines covered**. The tests are thorough, they just almost never run.
- Two Critical bugs were able to hide here (see the ranger factor-split and probability-forest-guard issues).

`codecov.yml` sets `informational: true` on both project and patch with a 1% threshold, so nothing about this ever blocked a PR.

**Ask.** Work out what the platform-specific failure actually was — most likely snapshot output that varies with ranger's RNG or numeric formatting across platforms — and make the assertions platform-independent by comparing against `ranger::predict()` with a tolerance instead of snapshotting. Then remove all 46 `skip_on_os()` calls, which also makes the reported coverage number real.

While here: `R/model-ranger.R:135-267` is dead legacy code. `get_child_info()`, `get_ra_path()`, `get_ra_tree()` and `get_ra_trees()` are self-documented as unused, and only `test-model-ranger.R:393-583` calls them. `get_ra_path()` also has latent bugs (`path[1:length(path) - 1]`, and `op` left undefined if neither `lc` nor `lr` matches). Deleting the functions and their tests would remove ~130 lines and ~10 test blocks.

---

# Priority 3 — robustness, documentation, infrastructure

title: Documentation gaps: `\value`, `@keywords internal` typo, stale model lists
description:
- [ ] **`@keywords internal` is silently ignored at `R/tree.R:112`, `:175`, `:204`.** The tag is written `#'  @keywords internal` with **two** spaces after `#'`, so roxygen treats it as continuation text of the preceding `@param` rather than a tag. Two consequences: the literal string `@keywords internal` is rendered inside the argument description (visible in `man/path_formula.Rd`, `man/path_formulas.Rd`, `man/generate_tree_node.Rd`), and those three topics are **not** marked internal, so they appear in the auto-generated pkgdown reference index despite not being exported.
- [ ] **Missing `\value` on 9 exported topics**: `tidypredict_fit`, `tidypredict_interval`, `tidypredict_test`, `tidypredict_to_column`, `tidypredict_sql`, `tidypredict_sql_interval`, `acceptable_formula`, `as_parsed_model`, `tidy.pm_regression`. Only `parse_model.Rd` and `set_catboost_categories.Rd` have one. CRAN incoming checks flag missing `\value` for exported functions even when local `R CMD check` is silent.
- [ ] **`man/tidypredict_test.Rd`** (the `model` param) says "It currently supports lm(), glm() and randomForest() models". NAMESPACE has 40+ `tidypredict_test` methods. Drop the enumeration.
- [ ] **`man/parse_model.Rd`** "Model types" lists only `pm_regression`, `pm_tree`, `pm_xgb`, `pm_lgb`, `pm_catboost`, but NAMESPACE also dispatches on `pm_bart`, `pm_naive_bayes`, `pm_nnet`, `pm_multiclass_regression` and `pm_nullmodel_classification`. Complete it, or say the list is non-exhaustive.
- [ ] **`README.md:95-132` "Supported models" is badly stale**: it lists 12 families and omits everything added in the dev version (C5.0, bagger, bart, cforest, fda/lda/qda/sda/sparsediscrim, ksvm, LiblineaR, mboost, mixOmics, multinom, naivebayes, nnet, nullmodel, quantreg, aorsf, h2o, xrf). The parsnip subsection lists 9 engines against ~30 supported. Replace both with a link to the pkgdown Model list so there is one place to update. `README.Rmd:104` "Elastic net models" is also better as "Regularized regression models", since glmnet now covers Cox and multinomial.
- [ ] **Missing `@examples`** on `as_parsed_model`, `tidypredict_to_column` and `tidy.pm_regression`; the first and third also have one-line descriptions that merely repeat the title ("Prepares parsed model object", "Tidy the parsed model results"). `tidypredict_to_column()` in particular is a headline function.
- [ ] `man/set_catboost_categories.Rd:32` holds the only `\dontrun{}` in the package. It is justified (catboost is not on CRAN), but `@examplesIf rlang::is_installed("catboost")` is the modern equivalent and would actually exercise the code where catboost exists.
- [ ] `R/parsemodel.R:29-33` lists cubist among the version-3 *nested* `case_when()` models, but `build_tree_formula.pm_tree_cubist` (`R/model-cubist.R:156-158`) routes to the flat rule-averaging builder.
- [ ] `R/tidypredict-package.R:24-25` has a stray `NULL` after `"_PACKAGE"`.

Two design questions rather than defects:

- The ~21 dot-prefixed exports (`.extract_*`, `.build_*`, `.c50_tree_info_full`, …) are all correctly `@keywords internal` and each is preceded by a `# For {orbital}` comment, so the arrangement is intentional and defensible. But the docs are one-line stubs ("For use in orbital package.") with no `@returns`, so a caller cannot tell what shape comes back, and there is no umbrella topic saying this family is an orbital-only contract with no stability guarantee. Adding `@returns` to each plus one `@family orbital helpers` would fix that. If orbital could call these via `:::` instead, un-exporting would shrink the public API surface by 21 topics.
- `_pkgdown.yml` has no `reference:` section, so the index is auto-generated and flat, currently mixing the core verbs with `generate_tree_node` / `path_formula` / `path_formulas` (see the first item). An explicit section with groups — Predict, Parse and serialize, SQL, Testing — would also make `pkgdown::check_pkgdown()` a real regression test for newly added topics.

title: tidypredict_test() fails for multiclass h2o models whose class labels look like numbers
description:
Found while sweeping h2o algorithms for #284.

`tidypredict_test.H2OMultinomialModel()` in `R/model-h2o.R` builds its comparison matrix with

```r
base_matrix <- as.matrix(preds[, domain, drop = FALSE])
```

where `domain` comes from `h2o_response_domain()`, i.e. the outcome factor's levels. But `h2o.predict()` does not always name the probability columns after the levels: when a level is not a syntactically valid name, h2o prefixes it with `p`. For an outcome whose levels are `"3"`, `"4"`, `"5"` the returned frame has columns `predict`, `p3`, `p4`, `p5`, and the subset fails with `undefined columns selected`.

Reproduce:

```r
library(h2o)
h2o.init()
df <- mtcars
df$gear <- factor(df$gear)
m <- h2o.gbm(x = setdiff(names(df), "gear"), y = "gear",
             training_frame = as.h2o(df), ntrees = 5)
tidypredict_test(m, df)
#> Error in `[.data.frame`(preds, , domain, drop = FALSE) :
#>   undefined columns selected
```

Relabelling the levels `g3`/`g4`/`g5` makes the same model pass at a max abs diff of 1.5e-09, so this is only the column lookup, not the formula: `tidypredict_fit()` is correct either way.

The fix is to select the probability columns positionally, or to match `domain` against the column names allowing for the `p` prefix, rather than assuming the two agree.

title: C5.0 boosted models (trials > 1) return the wrong class for newdata with NA
description:
Found by the agent that fixed #387 (PR #405), and explicitly left out of scope there.

PR #405 made single-tree C5.0 models handle `NA` in newdata correctly, by descending every branch weighted by each branch's share of training cases and taking an argmax. Boosted models (`trials > 1`) still mismatch `C50::predict.C5.0()` on **29 of 400 rows**.

## Severity

Silent: no error, no warning, just a different class. Lower priority than the rule-based case filed alongside this, only because that one sits behind the `C5_rules()` parsnip engine.

## Mechanism

The same root cause as #387: a missing split value must descend every branch weighted by training-case share rather than falling through to `.default`. PR #405 fixed that for a single tree. It was not extended to boosting because each trial produces its own weighted class distribution, and the ensemble combines them with per-trial confidence weights before the final argmax. So the correct expression needs a per-trial argmax plus confidence, which is substantially larger than the single-tree case.

## Fix direction

Unverified. Read how `predict.C5.0()` combines trials in `src/classify.c` before implementing, in particular whether the combination is over class votes or over weighted distributions, and where the per-trial confidence comes from.

Heed the expression-size lesson from PR #405: the obvious single `case_when()` nesting both subtrees under both arms doubles the expression at every tree level and is exponential in depth. That fix used `w * left + (1 - w) * right` with `w = case_when(is.na(x) ~ cases_left/cases, cond ~ 1, .default = 0)` to stay linear. Multiplying that across trials needs the same care, since a boosted model can carry many trees.

An informative abort when a boosted model is given `NA`-containing newdata is an acceptable resolution, and is better than the current silent divergence.

## Verifying a fix

Verify numerically against `C50::predict.C5.0()`, not structurally, and confirm the tests fail with the fix reverted. Sweep trial counts as well as class counts and `NA` placements.

title: ranger: respect.unordered.factors = "partition" gives wrong predictions on complete data
description:
Found by the agent working on #394 (PR #412), while reading ranger's split handling. Unrelated to #394's missing-value work and deliberately left alone there.

A `ranger` forest fit with `respect.unordered.factors = "partition"` disagrees with `predict()` by up to **0.038** on complete rows, with **no `NA` anywhere** in either the training data or the newdata.

## Severity

This is the most concerning shape a defect in this package can take: an ordinary documented option, ordinary complete data, no degenerate fit, no error and no warning, just a different number. Nothing about the call looks unusual, so a user has no signal that the generated formula and `predict()` have diverged.

## Mechanism

Unverified beyond localising it. With `respect.unordered.factors = "partition"` ranger does not order factor levels; it searches over subsets and stores the chosen subset as a **bitmask** in `splitValues`. `src/Tree.cpp` `Tree::predict()` takes the bitmask branch for these splits rather than the ordered comparison branch. The parser appears to be reading the stored split value as if it were an ordered threshold.

Note the related finding from #394: the bitmask branch is also the one that never consults the learned missing-value default direction, because that is only read for `isOrderedVariable` splits. Both observations point at the same code path being handled as if it were the ordered one.

## Fix direction

Unverified. Decode the bitmask into an explicit set membership test (`f %in% c(...)`) rather than a threshold comparison. Confirm against `src/Tree.cpp` which bit corresponds to which level, and in particular whether the bit order follows the factor's level order or ranger's internal recoding.

An informative abort is an acceptable resolution if the level correspondence turns out not to be recoverable from the fitted object, as was the case for ksvm in #390/PR #404.

## Verifying a fix

Per `CONTRIBUTING.md`, verify numerically against `predict.ranger()`, not structurally, and confirm the test fails with the fix reverted. Sweep several level counts and tree depths rather than testing a single fit, since a 0.038 diff on one model is easy to fix accidentally without fixing the class of problem.

title: lightgbm: dropped trees shift multiclass class assignment silently
description:
Found by the agent working on #401 (PR #407), which fixes this as a side effect of its stump work.

**This issue is filed for the record even though PR #407 resolves it.** It was never tracked separately, it is more likely to be hit in practice than the all-stump case that led to it, and if #407 is ever reverted or reworked this is the part that must not be lost.

## The defect

`lgb.model.dt.tree()` silently drops bare-leaf trees. When it does, tidypredict receives fewer trees than the model has, and in a multiclass fit it assigned the remaining trees to classes **positionally**, so every class label after the gap shifted.

Concretely, in a 2-iteration 3-class fit where one class was unrepresented, `lgb.model.dt.tree()` returned tree indices `0 1 3 4`. Index 2 was dropped. tidypredict had 4 trees for 3 classes and mapped them in order.

| | class 1 | class 2 | class 3 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| tidypredict | 0.235 | 0.239 | 0.526 |
| `predict()` | 0.547 | 0.453 | 1e-15 |

## Why it matters more than #401

#401 needs an entirely degenerate model: every tree in the fit must be a stump. This needs only **one absent class**, which is an ordinary situation in a multiclass problem with imbalanced or filtered data. The failure is silent: no error, no warning, and the probabilities still sum to 1, so nothing looks wrong.

## Mechanism

Verified. `dump_model()`'s `tree_info` holds `num_leaves = 1` and a `tree_structure` of `list(leaf_value, leaf_count)` with **no `split_index`** for a bare-leaf tree. The absent `split_index` is the discriminator. `lgb.model.dt.tree()` omits such trees entirely, so `tree_index` has gaps, and any positional class assignment is wrong from the first gap onward.

## Resolution

PR #407 adds `add_lgb_stump_trees()`, which reads the JSON dump, rebuilds every dropped bare-leaf tree as the one-leaf row the parser already handles, and re-sorts by `tree_index`. Because the trees are restored, the positional assignment becomes correct again rather than needing separate index-based logic. Verified numerically against `predict()` for multiclass all-stump and multiclass partial-stump fits.

Note for anyone reworking this: restoring the trees and keying off `tree_index` are two different fixes. #407 does the former. If a future change stops restoring the dropped trees, the class assignment must be made index-aware instead, or this defect returns silently.

title: C5.0 rule-based models (C5_rules) return the wrong class for newdata with NA
description:
Found by the agent that fixed #387 (PR #405), and explicitly left out of scope there.

PR #405 made single-tree C5.0 models handle `NA` in newdata correctly. Rule-based models are a **different mechanism** and are still wrong: **65 of 400 rows mismatch** `C50::predict.C5.0()`.

This is reached through the documented parsnip engine `C5_rules()`, as well as directly via `C50::C5.0(..., rules = TRUE)`.

## Severity

Silent. No error, no warning, just a different class for roughly one row in six in the sweep above. `C5_rules()` is a real engine that people use, which is what makes this the highest priority of the three C5.0 follow-ups (see also the boosted-model and class-probability cases filed alongside this).

## Mechanism

Partially verified. The tree case that #405 fixed works by descending every branch weighted by each branch's share of training cases and taking an argmax. Rules do not have that structure. In C5.0's `src/` the relevant behaviour is that `FindOutcome()` returns **-1** for an unknown value, so a rule whose condition tests a missing attribute does not fire, and the prediction falls through differently from how the parser models it.

Confirm the exact fallthrough against the C sources before implementing: what happens to the accumulated class votes when a rule is skipped, and whether the default class is applied at the rule-set level or per rule.

## Fix direction

Unverified. Establish first whether the correct behaviour is expressible as a `case_when()` at all. If it requires accumulating votes across rules in a way that grows the expression multiplicatively, note the lesson from PR #405: the naive shape doubles the expression at every level and is exponential, and the fix there deliberately used `w * left + (1 - w) * right` to stay linear.

An informative abort when a rule-based model is given `NA`-containing newdata is an acceptable resolution and is much better than the current silent divergence.

## Verifying a fix

Verify numerically against `C50::predict.C5.0()`, not structurally, and confirm the tests fail with the fix reverted. PR #405 used a 40-model sweep across class counts, split types and `NA` placements; something similar is appropriate here.

title: ksvm matrix interface: a non-syntactic column name references a column that does not exist
description:
Found by the agent that fixed #390 (PR #404), and explicitly left out of scope there.

PR #404 dealt with non-syntactic factor level names on the ksvm **formula** interface. The same root cause reaches the **matrix** interface (`ksvm(x, y)` with a column named e.g. `a:b`), where it produces a different and worse failure.

## Mechanism

Verified as part of #390: kernlab never calls `make.names()` explicitly. `ksvm()` does

```r
df <- na.action(data.frame(y, x))
```

and `data.frame()`'s default `check.names = TRUE` is `make.names(..., unique = TRUE)`. That single line is the source of both the character mangling and the duplicate-name uniquification that PR #377 identified.

On the formula interface there is a `terms` object to compare against, which is what PR #404 used to detect the ambiguity and abort. On the matrix interface **there is no `terms` object at all**, so the fallback parser has nothing to check against and emits a reference to a column that does not exist in the user's data.

## Fix direction

Unverified, and note the constraint that decided #390: the original names are **not recoverable** from the fitted object. Every slot was scanned there. `xmatrix` carries only mangled names, `terms` has `dataClasses` but no `xlevels`, `scaling` is numeric, `lev` is the response, and `kcall` names the data without storing it. A stored `fc.d` is the `make.names()` image of `c.d`, `c:d`, `c d` and others, plus of a `make.unique()` collision suffix, so there is no choosable pre-image.

The likely correct resolution is therefore an informative abort, matching what PR #404 did for the formula path. The work is in finding a reliable signal for the matrix path given that there is no `terms` object to decompose against.

Accept the same cost PR #404 accepted and document it: a column name that genuinely contains a `.` will abort too, because it is indistinguishable from the names that mangle onto it. `make.names()` is the identity on syntactic names, so correct models stay untouched.

## Verifying a fix

Assert the abort, and confirm that matrix-interface models with syntactic column names are entirely unaffected and still match `kernlab::predict()`.

title: C5.0 class probabilities are not NA-aware
description:
Found by the agent that fixed #387 (PR #405), and explicitly left out of scope there.

PR #405 made the C5.0 **class** prediction handle `NA` in newdata correctly. `c50_classprob_tree_info()`, which drives the class **probability** output, was not made `NA`-aware and still routes a missing split value to `.default`.

## Severity

Silent, like the rest of this family, but narrower than the two cases filed alongside this: it affects probability output rather than the predicted class, so a consumer taking an argmax may still land on the right answer while the probabilities themselves are wrong.

## Mechanism

The same root cause as #387. On a missing tested attribute C5.0 descends every branch weighted by that branch's share of training cases; the generated `case_when()` instead sends `NA` to `.default`, because `NA <= cut` is `NA` and `NA %in% ...` is `FALSE`.

The agent that fixed #387 gives the target value explicitly: the correct class probability is

```
(W * S_c + prior_c) / (W + 1)
```

with `W` the weighted leaf-count recursion and `S_c` the accumulated weighted class distribution. Confirm this against `src/classify.c` before implementing rather than taking it on trust, since it was noted in passing rather than verified as part of that PR's numeric work.

## Fix direction

Unverified. The machinery PR #405 added for the class case (each node's class distribution plus its two branches' case counts, recorded on `tree_info`) is very likely reusable here, which should make this the cheapest of the three C5.0 follow-ups. Reuse the same `w * left + (1 - w) * right` shape so the expression stays linear in tree depth rather than exponential.

Note that PR #405 put the new fields on `tree_info` specifically so that older parsed models fall back safely; preserve that property.

## Verifying a fix

Verify numerically against `predict(model, newdata, type = "prob")`, not structurally, and confirm the tests fail with the fix reverted.

title: Ordered factors are accepted through the parsnip path and read as levels
description:
Found by the per-model edge-case battery (PR #388), recorded there as skips.

`lda`, `qda` and `fda` reject an ordered factor, because `contr.poly` produces `.L`/`.Q` columns the parser cannot decompose. Reached through **parsnip**, the same fits are accepted, and the `.L`/`.Q` columns are then read as if they were level names.

| Model | Max abs diff vs `predict()` |
| --- | --- |
| `sda` | **0.79** |
| `sparsediscrim` | **0.49** |
| `mixOmics` | **1.34** |

So the guard exists and works on the direct path, and the parsnip path routes around it.

## Fix direction

Unverified. The question to answer first is whether the parsnip dispatch should be reaching `acceptable_formula()`/`acceptable_contrasts()` at all and is simply skipping it, or whether it reaches a different code path that predates the guard. PR #377 added `preproc_fields()` in `R/tidymodels.R` to pass `model$preproc` through to the `sda`/`sparsediscrim`/`mixOmics` parsers, which is the natural place to look.

Note the correct outcome here may be an abort rather than support: `contr.poly` decomposition was judged not worth supporting on the direct path, and consistency argues for the same answer, not the opposite one.

title: sparsediscrim and mixOmics: label collision and NA handling through parsnip
description:
Found by the per-model edge-case battery (PR #388), all recorded there as skips.

- [ ] **`sparsediscrim` label collision.** Level `y2` of factor `g` against a predictor named `gy2`: max abs diff **0.84**. This is the #376 case. PR #377 wired the plumbing but could not assert it, because the matrix interface's own `predict()` errors. **The workaround is the formula interface** (`lda_diag(cls ~ g + gy2, df)`), which fits and whose `predict()` works, so this is now verifiable and testable.
- [ ] **`mixOmics` unused factor level.** `tidypredict_fit()` errors with `missing value where TRUE/FALSE needed` while `predict()` succeeds.
- [ ] **`mixOmics` newdata containing `NA`.** `predict()` fills the value in; the generated formula returns `NA`.

## Context

PR #377 fixed the coefficient-label collision for seven models and reported `sparsediscrim` as "plumbing wired in but unasserted" precisely because no reference was available. Finding the formula-interface workaround closes that gap, so the first box should now be straightforward to both fix and test.

## Fix direction

Unverified for all three. For the collision, `term_fields()` and `preproc_fields()` (PRs #374 and #377) are the existing machinery. The two `mixOmics` items are independent of it.

title: Two ignored options in ensemble parsers: randomForest corr.bias and baguette C5.0 fuzzyThreshold
description:
Found by the per-model edge-case battery (PR #392), both recorded there as skips. Grouping them because they are the same shape of fix: an argument that changes `predict()` output and that the parser never reads.

- [ ] **`randomForest(corr.bias = TRUE)`** — `predict()` rescales the result using `model$coefs`, which the parser never consults. Max abs diff **0.21**.
- [ ] **`baguette` + C5.0 with `fuzzyThreshold = TRUE`** — soft thresholds blend adjacent branches; the generated formula uses hard splits. **3 of 150** iris rows misclassified.

## Why these survived

Category 4 of the new `CONTRIBUTING.md` battery ("options the parser might ignore") exists for exactly this, and the sweep that found these was the first time anyone enumerated each package's prediction-affecting arguments and checked them against the parser source rather than testing defaults.

Every ignored-option bug found so far has been in an ensemble or boosting library: LightGBM's `sigmoid`, `reg_sqrt` and `zero_as_missing` (#288), catboost objective links (#356), glmnet offsets, mboost `mstop`, and now these two.

## Fix direction

Unverified for both. Note the #288 precedent: two of its four proposed fixes would have been regressions, because `cross_entropy` accepts `sigmoid` without applying it and `huber` accepts `reg_sqrt` without acting on it. Confirm that each argument actually changes `predict()` output before making the parser react to it.

title: ranger: training data containing NA gives wrong predictions
description:
Found by the per-model edge-case battery (PR #392), recorded there as a `skip()`.

ranger routes `NA` **per node**, while the generated formula always sends `NA` left. Max abs diff **1.48**, and the disagreement falls on exactly the rows containing `NA`; complete rows are exact.

## This is the third instance of one pattern

The same shape has now been found three times, each in a different backend:

- **#288** LightGBM: `default_left` is consulted only when `missing_type` is `NaN`, so a feature with no NA in training routes differently (fixed, PR #347)
- **#387** C5.0: descends every branch and combines by branch frequency, formula routes to `.default`
- **this one** ranger: per-node NA routing, formula routes left

In every case the existing tests covered `NA` in *newdata* only, or trained without `NA`, which is the one regime where the naive handling is correct. Category 2 of the `CONTRIBUTING.md` battery now requires both regimes precisely because of this.

## Fix direction

Unverified, and worth checking against the ranger source before implementing. The LightGBM fix (PR #347) had to join per-node routing metadata that was absent from the convenient accessor and only present in the full model dump; ranger may need the same treatment.

title: xrf: a variable named like another factor's dummy produces all NA
description:
Found by the per-model edge-case battery (PR #392), recorded there as a `skip()`.

With a factor `cyl` (levels 4/6/8) alongside a separate variable literally named `cyl4`, `xrf_feature_field()` checks `feature %in% vars` **before** matching levels, so the `cyl4` dummy is emitted as the raw column. The generated expression becomes `cyl4 * 1.6156`, which raises a factor-arithmetic warning and evaluates to **all `NA`**.

Requires `sparse = FALSE`; xrf itself refuses the sparse variant.

## Related

This is the same collision family as #376 (fixed for seven models in PR #377) and #290 before it, but `xrf` has its own field resolver and so was untouched by both. That is now the **third** time this helper-shared defect has been found in a parser that had its own copy of the logic, which is the pattern recorded in `CONTRIBUTING.md`: for a defect in shared decomposition logic, the file list in the issue is a starting point, never the scope.

## Fix direction

Unverified. The ordering in `xrf_feature_field()` is the immediate cause, but PR #374/#377 established that matching on the model's `assign` attribute and `xlevels` beats string matching for exactly this class of bug; worth checking whether `term_fields()` can serve here rather than reordering two string checks.

title: lightgbm: an all-stump model errors with "Model has no trees"
description:
Found by the per-model edge-case battery (PR #400), which completes the battery across all 32 `test-model-*.R` files. Not committed as a failing test.

When LightGBM cannot make a single split it stops boosting after one iteration and emits a model whose only tree is a bare leaf. `lightgbm::lgb.model.dt.tree()` returns **zero rows** for such a model, so `parse_model()` produces `trees = list()` and `tidypredict_fit()` aborts at `R/model-lightgbm.R:637` with `"Model has no trees."` LightGBMs own `predict()` works fine and returns the constant.

## Reproducing

```r
X <- cbind(x1 = rnorm(50), x2 = rnorm(50))
p <- list(objective = "regression", num_leaves = 4L, learning_rate = 0.3, min_data_in_leaf = 1L)
ds <- lightgbm::lgb.Dataset(X, label = rep(5, 50), params = p)
m <- lightgbm::lgb.train(params = p, data = ds, nrounds = 3L, verbose = -1L)

m$current_iter()                        # 1
nrow(lightgbm::lgb.model.dt.tree(m))    # 0
predict(m, X)                           # 5 for every row
tidypredict_fit(m)                      # Error: Model has no trees.
```

The JSON dump does carry the information: `tree_info` holds one tree with `num_leaves = 1` and `leaf_value = 5`. Only `lgb.model.dt.tree()` drops it.

Two further configurations hit the same path: single-row training data, and the plain bonsai default `boost_tree(trees = 5, tree_depth = 3, min_n = 1)` on a lone 4-level factor, where LightGBMs categorical guards (`min_data_per_group`, `cat_smooth`) reject every split. That last one is an ordinary parsnip call on small data, so this is reachable without contriving anything.

## Why the existing test did not catch it

`test-model-lightgbm.R` has a test named *"single leaf tree (stump) has empty path"*, but it hand-builds a `tree_df` containing one leaf row. Real `lgb.model.dt.tree()` never returns that shape for a stump model: it returns nothing at all. The test asserts against a fixture that cannot occur.

## Relation to #397

Same family, different mechanism, so filed separately. #397 is four backends returning a correct value with the wrong *length*; this one errors outright and produces no value. A fix for #397 will not reach it, because the failure happens earlier, at parse time rather than at evaluation.

## Fix direction

Unverified. Reading the stump leaf value from the JSON dump rather than from `lgb.model.dt.tree()` is the obvious candidate.

title: All-stump models return a length-1 result instead of one value per row
description:
Found by the per-model edge-case battery (PR #392), recorded there as a `skip()`.

When every tree in a model is a stump, the generated formula references no column at all, so `rlang::eval_tidy()` returns a scalar rather than a vector of length `nrow(newdata)`.

**Affected:** ranger, baguette, xgboost, xrf.
**Immune:** randomForest and aorsf, which route through `expr_na_if_incomplete()` and so still reference a column.

## Severity: low, and deliberately so

The computed **value is correct**, and `dplyr::mutate()` recycles a length-1 column, so `tidypredict_to_column()` on a data frame gives the right answer. It bites when the expression is evaluated directly, or where recycling is not applied.

Filing it rather than ignoring it because the silent-length-mismatch shape is how #310's stump bugs originally presented, and because a caller checking `length(result) == nrow(data)` would see a failure with no error.

## Note for whoever picks this up

The battery agent that found this initially reported six *other* failures in this same area that turned out to be its own test-construction error: degenerate fits correctly collapse to a scalar, and it had compared that scalar against `predict()`'s recycled vector. Values matched exactly and only lengths differed. Be careful to distinguish "the parser produced a scalar where a vector was required" from "the test forgot to recycle".

## Fix direction

Unverified. `expr_na_if_incomplete()` already produces the correct shape for the two immune models, so extending that treatment is the obvious first thing to evaluate.

title: C5.0: newdata with NA returns the wrong class
description:
Found by the per-model edge-case battery (PR #386), which recorded it as a `skip()` rather than a failing assertion.

C5.0 descends **every** branch when a split value is missing, then combines the leaf class distributions weighted by branch frequency. The generated `case_when()` instead routes `NA` to `.default`, so a row whose fractional descent favours one class can come back as another.

## Reproducer

`mtcars` with `cyl` blanked out, 4 of 32 rows flip: tidypredict returns `"0"` where `predict()` returns `"1"` at probability 0.523. That is a genuine fractional descent, not a tie-break that happens to land the other way.

See `tests/testthat/test-model-C5.0.R` for the skipped case with the full reproducer.

## Why this survived

The existing C5.0 tests covered missing values only in the *training* data, not in newdata. This is the same shape as the LightGBM `missing_type` bug in #288: the suite exercised the one regime where the naive handling happens to be correct.

## Fix direction

Unverified, and per `CONTRIBUTING.md` it should be checked against the C5.0 source before being implemented. Reproducing the weighted multi-branch descent in a `case_when()` may not be expressible in general, in which case the honest outcome is a documented limitation plus an abort or warning rather than a silently different class.

title: ksvm: non-syntactic factor level names give silently wrong predictions
description:
Found by the per-model edge-case battery (PR #388), recorded there as a `skip()` with a reproducer.

`make.names()` turns a level `c:d` into `fc.d`, and the generated formula then emits `f == "c.d"`, a comparison that never matches the actual data.

| Fit | Max abs diff vs `predict()` |
| --- | --- |
| regression | **0.90** |
| classification | **0.75** |

This is the highest-impact of the six defects that sweep turned up, because it is silent: no error, no warning, just a different number.

Related but distinct from #376/PR #377, which fixed *label collision* in the same file. This one is about level names that are not syntactically valid, so the round trip through `make.names()` loses information.

## Fix direction

Unverified. Per `CONTRIBUTING.md`, check against the kernlab source before implementing: the parser needs to recover the original level, not the `make.names()` image, and PR #377 established that kernlab also uniquifies duplicate model matrix column names, so both transformations may need undoing.

title: lda and qda wrongly reject a factor level containing a colon
description:
Found by the per-model edge-case battery (PR #388), recorded there as a `skip()`.

`acceptable_contrasts()` splits model matrix column names on `:` to separate interaction terms, so a factor level whose *name* contains `:` is misread and the fit is rejected.

This is a false rejection, not a wrong number: the model is fine. Bypassing the check gives **2e-16** agreement with `predict()`, and `fda` accepts exactly the same data through a different path.

## Fix direction

Unverified. The decomposition needs to distinguish a `:` that separates interaction terms from a `:` inside a level name. PR #374 added `term_fields()` (originally `lm_fields()`) in `R/model-lm.R`, which drives decomposition from the model's `assign` attribute and `xlevels` rather than from string splitting, and PR #377 extended it to several more models. That machinery already solves this class of problem and is the natural place to look first.

title: LightGBM: four ignored parameters (`missing_type`, `zero_as_missing`, `sigmoid`, `reg_sqrt`)
description:
Four parameters that change LightGBM's own prediction are not consulted by the parser. Same file and same shape of fix, so grouping them.

- [ ] **`missing_type` is ignored, so NA routing is wrong for models trained without NA — the common case.** `R/model-lightgbm.R:314-330`, `:666-674`. tidypredict routes NA purely by `default_left`, but LightGBM's `Tree::NumericalDecision` consults `default_left` **only** when the node's `missing_type` is `NaN` (or `Zero`). When `missing_type == None` — which is what you get for *any feature with no NA in the training data* — LightGBM coerces NaN to `0.0` and compares it against the threshold normally.

  Repro: feature `neg ~ Uniform(-10,-5)`, regression, 6 rounds, no NA in training. All 21 splits on `neg` have `default_left = TRUE` and negative thresholds, so NaN→0 goes **right** in LightGBM and **left** in tidypredict:
  ```
  maxdiff = 8.250763
    lgb:         -10.4248  -11.05753  -10.91728
    tidypredict: -18.13758 -19.0575   -18.13758
  lgb pred for NA == lgb pred for 0 ?  diff = 0   # confirms the NaN->0 semantics
  ```
  Both the nested and v3 flat builders are affected. **The current tests miss this because they all train *with* NA** (`test-model-lightgbm.R:412,890,1590` use `use_missing = TRUE` on NA-containing data), which yields `missing_type = NaN` — the one case where `default_left` happens to be correct.

  `missing_type` is available per node in `model$dump_model()` but **not** in `lgb.model.dt.tree()`, so it has to be joined by `tree_index`/`split_index`. Then emit: `NaN` → current behaviour; `None` → `dplyr::coalesce(col, 0) <= t`, ignoring `default_left`; `Zero` → next item.

- [ ] **`zero_as_missing` is ignored.** With `zero_as_missing = TRUE` every node gets `missing_type = "Zero"`, and LightGBM routes **both NA and exact 0** to the `default_left` side; tidypredict compares zeros against the threshold. Regression with 40 zeros injected into `x2` plus a categorical feature is wrong **on the training data itself**: 1.30847, and the same on new zeros and on NA. Data-dependent — a simpler configuration gave 0. Fix: emit `(is.na(col) | col == 0) | col <= t` when `default_left`, else `!is.na(col) & col != 0 & col <= t`.

- [ ] **`reg_sqrt` is ignored.** `:435-453`, `lgb_identity_objectives` at `:3-11`. `objective = "regression"` with `reg_sqrt = TRUE` trains on `sqrt(|y|)`, and `RegressionL2loss::ConvertOutput` returns `sign(x) * x^2`; tidypredict treats it as identity. mtcars mpg, 5 rounds: **max abs diff 25.09**, larger than the response. Fix: in `apply_lgb_objective()`, when the objective is in `lgb_identity_objectives` and `isTRUE(params$reg_sqrt)`, return `expr(sign(!!f) * !!f^2)`; if the flag cannot be read reliably from a reloaded model, abort.

- [ ] **`sigmoid` is ignored.** `:370-372`, `:447-449`, `:393-394`. LightGBM's `binary`, `cross_entropy` (via `BinaryLogloss`) and `multiclassova` apply `1/(1+exp(-sigmoid * x))`; `lgb_sigmoid()` hardcodes 1. With `sigmoid = 2`: **max abs diff 0.1499** on a probability scale. Fix: pass `params$sigmoid %||% 1` and emit `1 / (1 + exp(-(s * f)))` on both the binary and `multiclassova` paths.

Two cleanups in the same area: `:436-440` is a dead `if` block with an empty body (the `rf` division happens in `assemble_lgb_formula()` at `:520-522`), and the `default_left == TRUE` branch for `decision_type == "=="` (`:336-341`, `:678-681`) is unreachable and would be wrong if reached — `CategoricalDecision` always sends NaN and negative values right, and `Tree::SplitCategorical` never sets the bit (confirmed empirically: 8 categorical splits, `default_left TRUE: 0`).

title: catboost inverts the link for Logloss but not for Poisson or Tweedie
description:
Found by the ignored-fit-options battery.

## What happens

`R/model-catboost.R:3-14` puts `Poisson` and `Tweedie` in `catboost_identity_objectives`, so `tidypredict_fit()` returns the raw formula value on the log scale. `Logloss` and `CrossEntropy` are in `catboost_sigmoid_objectives` and get a logistic applied.

Those two choices follow different conventions, and only one can match a given `catboost.predict()` call:

| Objective | tidypredict | matches `RawFormulaVal` (catboost's **default**) | matches `Probability` / `Exponent` |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `Poisson` | identity | **yes, 0 difference** | no, 1.457 off `Exponent` |
| `Logloss` | sigmoid | no | **yes, 0 difference** |

So a user who fits `Logloss` gets probabilities, and a user who fits `Poisson` gets log-counts. Neither is wrong on its own terms; together they are inconsistent, and nothing documents which convention applies to which objective.

`xgboost` takes the other convention throughout: `apply_xgb_objective()` (`R/model-xgboost.R:327`) applies `exp()` for `count:poisson`, `reg:tweedie` and `reg:gamma`, matching what `predict()` returns for those objectives. So the same fitted model shape gets a link inverted through the xgboost path and not through the catboost path.

## Measured

20-iteration depth-4 model, Poisson objective, 200 rows:

```
RawFormulaVal  max abs diff vs tidypredict 0
Exponent       max abs diff vs tidypredict 1.457
Probability    max abs diff vs tidypredict 0.652
```

Also swept and clean: `Logloss` (0), `MAE` (0), `boosting_type = "Ordered"` (0).

## The decision

Which convention should catboost follow? Either is arguable:

- **Invert the link for `Poisson` and `Tweedie` too**, matching xgboost and giving predictions on the response scale. Diverges from `catboost.predict()`'s default, as `Logloss` already does.
- **Leave the raw value and drop the sigmoid from `Logloss`**, matching `catboost.predict()`'s default everywhere. Consistent, but changes existing behaviour for the far more common objective and would surprise anyone using it for classification.

The first looks right to me, since the sigmoid for `Logloss` has presumably been relied on, but it is a behaviour change either way and worth deciding deliberately. Whichever is chosen, the objective-to-link mapping should be documented, since it cannot be inferred from `catboost.predict()`'s own default.

title: LightGBM: a parsed linear-tree model cannot be fitted
description:
`tidypredict_fit()` works on a `linear_tree = TRUE` LightGBM model directly, but errors once the model has been through `parse_model()`:

```r
library(lightgbm)
set.seed(1)
n <- 500
d <- data.frame(x1 = runif(n, -10, -5), x2 = rnorm(n), x3 = rnorm(n),
                cat = sample(0:4, n, TRUE))
d$y <- 2 * d$x1 + d$x2 - d$x3 + d$cat + rnorm(n)

p <- list(objective = "regression", verbose = -1L, num_leaves = 8L,
          linear_tree = TRUE)
ds <- lgb.Dataset(as.matrix(d[c("x1","x2","x3","cat")]), label = d$y,
                  categorical_feature = 4L, params = p)
m <- lgb.train(params = p, data = ds, nrounds = 8L)

rlang::eval_tidy(tidypredict_fit(m), d)           # fine, max diff 3.6e-15
rlang::eval_tidy(tidypredict_fit(parse_model(m)), d)
#> Error in `case_when()`:
#> ! `..1 (right)` must be a vector, not `NULL`.
```

`get_lgb_tree()` sets `prediction = NULL` for any leaf that has linear information, storing the coefficients under `linear` instead. The parsed-model builder reaches that leaf through `build_nested_from_flat_paths()` (`R/tree-nested.R:352`, `:370`, `:375`), which reads `leaves[[i]]$prediction` and never looks at `linear`, so `NULL` reaches `case_when()`.

The example above is the simplest failing case: the leaf that trips it has **no** linear terms at all (`feature_names` is `chr(0)`), just an intercept, so even a constant leaf inside a linear tree is lost. Leaves that do carry coefficients would be dropped the same way.

This also means a linear-tree model saved with `tidypredict_save()` cannot be loaded and used, since the saved leaf has a null prediction.

**Fix direction.** The parsed path needs the same `build_lgb_linear_prediction()` treatment the direct path applies in `build_nested_lgb_node()`, or `build_nested_from_flat_paths()` needs a hook for turning a leaf into an expression rather than reading `$prediction` directly. The latter would also serve catboost and xgboost, which pass through the same function.

Found while sweeping LightGBM's missing-value parameters for #288; unrelated to missing values, and present before that work.

title: Missing input validation on the exported API
description:
Several exported functions accept invalid input and produce corrupt output or a base-R error instead of a clear message.

- [ ] `tidypredict_to_column()` does not validate `vars` (`R/predict-column.R:36-38`). `tidypredict_to_column(mtcars, m, add_interval = TRUE, vars = "f")` returns a data frame whose last column is literally named `NA`. Add `if (length(vars) != 3) cli::cli_abort(...)`, and validate that `interval` is a single number in (0, 1) and `add_interval` is a scalar logical.
- [ ] The `interval` argument is unvalidated everywhere (`R/predict-interval.R:17`, `R/to_sql.R:33`). `tidypredict_interval(m, 1.5)` returns an expression beginning with `NaN`, plus a bare `qt()` warning; `interval = 0` returns `0 * sqrt(...)`. Check numeric, length 1, strictly within (0, 1), with `cli_abort(call = caller_env())`.
- [ ] `as_parsed_model.list()` has no validation (`R/as-parsed-model.R:11-15`). `as_parsed_model(list())` yields class `c("parsed_model", "pm_", "list")` with no error, and downstream failures are then obscure. Abort when `x$general$type` is missing or not a scalar string.
- [ ] `parse_model()` and `acceptable_formula()` have no `.default` method (`R/parsemodel.R:56`, `R/acceptable.R:15`), so direct calls on unsupported objects give R's "no applicable method" error. `tidypredict_fit.default` already produces a good message; mirror it.
- [ ] `tidypredict_interval.list()` errors with a base error on a malformed parsed model (`R/predict-interval.R:38-48`): `if (mt == "lm")` with `mt` `NULL` gives "argument is of length zero". Also, since every parsed model inherits `"list"`, a `pm_tree` reaches this method and gets the terse "Model type not supported." rather than the informative `.default` message. Use `switch()` on `mt %||% ""` and reuse the `.default` wording.
- [ ] `tidypredict_sql()` returns a one-element **list** for intercept-only models (`R/to_sql.R:39-44`). `translate_fit()` special-cases only `inherits(f, "call")`, but builders can legitimately return a bare numeric: `tidypredict_sql(lm(mpg ~ 1, mtcars), simulate_dbi())` gives `[[1]] <SQL> 20.090625`. Same for `nullmodel` regression fits. Fix: branch on `is.list(f)` instead.
- [ ] `f32_split_boundary()` returns `NaN` for thresholds at or beyond the float range (`R/float32.R:39-65`). `f32_split_boundary(Inf, "upper")` → `NaN`; `1e40` → `NaN` (it overflows to `Inf`, then the bit-increment crosses into NaN space). A `NaN` boundary makes every comparison `FALSE`, so the model silently mispredicts rather than erroring. Leave non-finite and overflowing values untouched, or clamp.
- [ ] `as_f32()` silently corrupts integer input (`R/float32.R:22-24`). `writeBin(3L, raw(), size = 4)` writes an *integer* which is read back as a float, so `as_f32(3L)` is `4.203895e-45`. Latent today because both callers pass through `as.numeric()`, but a trap for the next caller. Coerce with `as.numeric(x)` inside.
- [ ] `cli::cli_abort()` is passed `call. = FALSE` at `R/acceptable.R:54`, `R/acceptable.R:94` and `R/model-ksvm.R:158`. cli takes `call`, not `call.`, so the argument is swallowed by `...` and errors are attributed to the internal helper. Thread `call = rlang::caller_env()` through properly.

title: Cubist: a ~0.1 residual on all-numeric training data, independent of committees
description:
Found while fixing #286 (PR #371). Separate defect, filing so it is not lost in that issue's thread.

## What

An all-numeric `Cubist::cubist()` fit disagrees with `Cubist::predict()` by about 0.1 (max abs diff) **on its own training data**. On fresh data the same models agree at ~3e-07.

## What it is not

- **Not committee-related.** The residual is constant at 5, 15 and 20 committees, and it survives the #286 fix that corrects committee assignment above 20. It is present at committee counts where #286 does not apply at all.
- **Not the #285 extrapolation clamp.** That landed in PR #340, and these measurements are from a tree that includes it.
- **Not shape-dependent in the usual way.** It appears on all-numeric data; the factor-predictor configurations measured alongside it sat at ~3e-07 on training data.

## Measurements

From the #286 reproduction sweep, 400 rows, max abs diff against `Cubist::predict()`, with the #286 fix applied:

| data | committees | training | fresh |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| numeric | 5 | ~0.1 | ~3e-07 |
| numeric | 15 | ~0.1 | ~3e-07 |
| numeric | 20 | ~0.1 | ~3e-07 |
| factor | 5 / 15 / 20 | ~3e-07 | ~3e-07 |

The training/fresh asymmetry is the interesting part and is probably the fastest route in: something differs specifically for rows the model was fit on. Cubist rules carry per-rule `loval`/`hival` bounds and an extrapolation clamp that PR #340 established "fires on ordinary training rows, not only on extrapolation", so that clamp is worth checking first even though the current implementation is verified to 1e-6 on 90 configurations.

## Why the batteries missed it

The threshold-precision battery recorded a precision ceiling for Cubist at 15 significant digits (see the triage plan), which is far below 0.1, so this is not that ceiling. No battery compared Cubist on training data specifically.

title: Stump trees crash the flat and exported tree builders
description:
- [ ] **`generate_case_when_tree()` crashes on a root-only tree.** `R/tree.R:64-69`. For a stump, `generate_tree_node()` returns a bare value (`path_formulas()` → `TRUE` → the early return at `:149-151`), and `rlang::f_rhs(default)` then aborts with `` `x` must be a formula ``. Reachable for any saved v1/v2 ranger or randomForest parsed model containing a stump, which ranger produces routinely (`ranger(y ~ x, d)` on a constant `y` gives a one-row `treeInfo`). Fix: copy the guard `.build_case_when_tree()` already has at `:275-277`.

- [ ] **`.build_case_when_tree()` emits invalid code for a non-numeric stump.** `:275` guards with `is.numeric(node_exprs[[1]])`, so a classification stump (`prediction = "a"`) falls through and produces `case_when(.default = "a")`, which dplyr rejects with `` `...` can't be empty ``. This function is exported for {orbital}. Fix: guard on `!rlang::is_formula(node_exprs[[1]])` instead.

- [ ] **`parsedmodel$general$mode` relies on `$` partial matching.** `:56`. ranger and randomForest parsed models have no `general$mode`, so `$mode` partially matches `general$model` and `calc_mode` silently becomes `"ranger"` / `"randomForest"`. It works only by accident, since any non-`"ifelse"` string behaves like `""` — but if the field were ever truly absent, `if (calc_mode == "ifelse")` at `:153` errors with "argument is of length zero". Fix: `parsedmodel$general[["mode"]] %||% ""`.

Lower-priority items in the same files, fine to fold in or skip:

- `path_formulas()` only recognizes `type = "all"` when it is the sole path element (`:181-185` vs `:205-217`); a mixed path aborts with the internal "unsupported value" error. Today's parsers never mix them, but `path_formula()` should just return `TRUE` for `"all"`.
- A single-element non-intercept `prediction` produces garbage (`:118` branches on `length(prediction) > 1` and the `else` branch only unwraps `is_intercept`), and an all-zero prediction list aborts in `reduce_addition()` with an empty-`.x` error (`:129-141`). Both are **unreachable from today's cubist parser**, which always keeps the intercept, so they matter only if another parser starts emitting that shape.
- Malformed tree info gives a cryptic base error at `R/tree-nested.R:65-68`: a dangling child id makes `node_idx` empty and `if (tree_info$terminal[node_idx])` throws "argument is of length zero". Use `cli::cli_abort(..., .internal = TRUE)` when `length(node_idx) != 1`.
- `split$is_categorical` is read bare at `R/tree-nested.R:110` while `is_oblique` and `strict` use `isTRUE()`; an absent field errors, and an empty `vals` yields `x %in% NULL`, sending everything to `.default`.
- `build_nested_from_paths_recursive()` trusts `leaves[[1]]` (`R/tree-nested.R:203-205`): when the first leaf's path is exhausted it returns that prediction and silently drops the remaining leaves. Unreachable for a well-formed tree, but an internal error would be safer than a silently truncated tree.
- `generate_case_when_tree(default =)` and `generate_case_when_trees(default =)` are never called with `FALSE` anywhere in `R/`.

title: Saved v1/v2 rpart and partykit parsed models return `NULL` invisibly
description:
`R/predict-fit.R:51-69` handles only `cubist`, `randomForest` and `ranger` in the version-1/2 branch. rpart and partykit models were serialized as `type = "tree", version = 2` (see `git show 6d102b3:R/model-rpart.R:378-381`, which stored `pm$trees`), and the flat builder for them has since been deleted. `tidypredict_fit()` therefore falls off the end of the `if` chain and returns `NULL` with no error:

```r
tidypredict_fit(structure(
  list(general = list(model = "rpart", version = 2, type = "tree")),
  class = c("parsed_model", "pm_tree", "list")
))
#> NULL
```

This defeats the backwards-compatibility promise documented at `R/parsemodel.R:35-37`.

**Fix.** Restore or re-route the v2 rpart/partykit path, and terminate the function with a `cli::cli_abort()` naming the model and version so that any future gap errors instead of returning `NULL`.

Related latent gap in the same function: `tidypredict_fit.pm_lgb` and `.pm_catboost` (`:116-123`) ignore `$version` entirely and always use the nested builder.

The backwards-compat fixtures should gain a v2 rpart and a v2 partykit case.

title: parse_label_lm(): multinom, nnet, earth and ksvm keep the coefficient-label collision bug
description:
Follow-up to #308, which PR #374 closes for `lm`, `glm` and `rq` only.

## What

PR #374 fixed ambiguous coefficient-label parsing by adding `lm_fields()`, which drives the decomposition from the model's `assign` attribute plus `attr(terms, "term.labels")` and `xlevels` rather than guessing from strings. It is wired in through the new `build_terms(fields = )` argument.

`multinom`, `nnet`, `earth` and `ksvm` call `parse_label_lm()` **directly**, passing only variable names, so they never reach the new code path and retain the original defect: a coefficient label that collides with another variable name is treated as an ordinary column.

## Measured

With PR #374 applied, `y ~ g + gy2` where `g` has a level `y2`, max abs diff against each model's own `predict()`:

| model | before #374 | after #374 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `lm` | 1.325 | 2.8e-17 |
| `glm` | 0.664 | 1.1e-16 |
| `rq` | 1.125 | 5.6e-17 |
| `multinom` | 1.0 | **1.0, unchanged** |
| `nnet` | | unfixed |
| `earth` | | unfixed |
| `ksvm` | | unfixed |

## Fix

Each of the four needs roughly a one-line change in its own parser file to pass `fields = ` through `build_terms()`, the hook PR #374 added for exactly this. `R/model-multinom.R`, `R/model-nnet.R`, `R/model-earth.R`, `R/model-ksvm.R`.

Note these models may not all have an `assign` attribute available; #374 handles that for `glm` and `rq` by rebuilding it from the model frame rather than the formula, so the fitting data need not still exist. The same approach should carry over.

## Why this was left open

The #308 fix was done in a worktree scoped to `R/model-lm.R` while other agents held the other model files, so it could not reach them. `parse_label_lm()` is shared by six consumers, and the last bug in this same helper (#290, PR #321) was verified against all six for precisely this reason.

title: `lm`: rank-deficient fits abort, and label parsing is ambiguous
description:
- [ ] **Rank-deficient (aliased) fits abort entirely, even though fitted values are well defined.** `R/model-lm.R:71-88` calls `qr.solve(qr.R(model$qr))` unconditionally in `parse_model_lm()`, so `tidypredict_fit()` — which needs no QR at all — fails too:
  ```r
  lm(mpg ~ cyl_f * gear_f, d)   # 1 NA coefficient
  tidypredict_fit(m)  #> Error: Unable to calculate inverse of QR decomposition.
  lm(mpg ~ wt + dup, d)         # exact duplicate column, same error
  ```
  `predict.lm()` handles both fine by dropping `NA` coefficients. Fix: drop `NA` coefficients, compute the QR from `model$qr$rank` columns only, and defer the abort to `tidypredict_interval()` where it is actually needed.
