Secondary: the `grepl("singular matrix", cnd$message)` test at `:75` depends on an untranslated English message, and `stop(cnd)` re-raises without the original call.

- [ ] **Label parsing is ambiguous, in two silently-wrong ways.** `:158`, `:166-169`.
  - Factor levels containing `:` are split as interactions. Level `"b:2"` becomes ``ifelse(g == "b", 1, 0) * `2` ``, which errors on evaluation.
  - A coefficient label that collides with another variable name is treated as an ordinary column, because of the `!(items[i] %in% vars)` guard: `lm(y ~ g + gy2)` with level `y2` gives **max abs diff 0.0391**.

  The robust fix is to stop string-guessing and drive the decomposition from `model$xlevels` plus `attr(model$terms, "term.labels")` / the `assign` attribute, which give the exact variable-to-level mapping. Abort if a level contains `:` and cannot be resolved unambiguously.

- [ ] **Prediction intervals ignore case weights.** `:225-234`. `predict.lm(interval = "prediction")` uses `res.var/weights` per row; tidypredict adds a constant `sigma2`. Weighted `lm(mpg~wt+disp, weights=w)` gives a **max upper-bound difference of 3.485**, while the QR/confidence part matches at 7e-15 — isolating the fault to the `+ sigma2` term. Fix: abort on non-constant `model$weights`, or document the limitation.

Related, lower priority: the probit approximation at `:52` gives max abs diff 1.414e-04 against `predict(type = "response")`, which exceeds the default `tidypredict_test()` threshold of 1e-12 and reports 32 records above it on a perfectly correct model. Only the unit test knows about the approximation (it uses `< 0.001`). This should be documented in the glm/lm and `tidypredict_test()` docs, and the inline comment "max error ~0.014%" is clearer stated as ~1.4e-4 absolute probability.

title: `acceptable_formula()` accepts every contrast once one field uses `contr.treatment`
description:
`R/acceptable.R:49`:

```r
contr <- contr[!("contr.treatment" %in% contr)]
```

`%in%` collapses to a single logical, so if *any* field uses treatment contrasts, the filter drops the whole vector and every other field's contrast is accepted.

```r
df <- mtcars; df$cyl <- factor(df$cyl); df$gear <- factor(df$gear)
m <- lm(mpg ~ wt + cyl + gear, data = df,
        contrasts = list(cyl = "contr.treatment", gear = "contr.poly"))
acceptable_formula(m)      # NULL, silent
tidypredict_test(m)$alert  # TRUE — fit_diff 0.730487 on every row
```

**Fix.**

```r
contr <- contr[!vapply(contr, identical, logical(1), "contr.treatment")]
```

Two adjacent nits in the same function: the error message at `:52-53` prints the contrast rather than the field ("Field(s) with an invalid contrast are: `contr.poly`" when the field is `gear`) — use `{.field {names(contr)}}`; and `:54` and `:94` pass `call. = FALSE` to `cli::cli_abort()`, which takes `call`, so the error is attributed to the internal helper (`Error in acceptable_lm()`).

title: cubist: rules are mis-assigned to committees above 20 committees
description:
`R/model-cubist.R:83-99` derives `ommittee_id` for `committees > 1` by parsing the "Number of rules per committee" line out of `capture.output(print(model))`. **`print.Cubist` truncates that list at 20 committees with `" ... "`.**

With `committees = 25` the line reads `Number of rules per committee: 23, 13, ..., 9 ... `, so `ommittee_id` has length 242 for 298 rules. `split()` then recycles it — emitting only a `data length is not a multiple of split variable` warning — and the committee divisor becomes 20 instead of 25.

| committees | parsed rules | `length(ommittee_id)` | distinct ids | max abs diff |
|------------|--------------|-----------------------|--------------|--------------|
| 1          | 23           | 23                    | 1            | 1.28e-2      |
| 2          | 36           | 36                    | 2            | 6.4e-3       |
| 10         | 132          | 132                   | 10           | 5.5e-2       |
| 25         | 298          | **242**               | **20**       | **0.668**    |
| 50         | 575          | **242**               | **20**       | **2.00**     |

**Fix.** Drop the print-scraping entirely. `model$coefficients` has one row per rule with a `committee` column, and `comm` is already built in exactly that row order (`unique(coefs$committee)`, then `coefs$rule[coefs$committee == comm]`), so:

```r
ommittee_id  <- as.integer(coefs$committee)
n_committees <- length(unique(coefs$committee))
```

Verified: with that substitution, `committees = 25` drops from **0.668 to 0.042** — the remainder is the missing extrapolation clamp, filed separately.

While here: the field name `ommittee_id` is missing its leading `c`. Renaming it is a parsed-model format change, so bundle it with the version bump for the extrapolation-clamp fix if that lands first.

Add a test at `committees = 25` or higher; every current test is at or below the truncation point.

title: aorsf: over half of training rows mispredict because oblique split thresholds are refolded
description:
Found by the threshold-precision battery. Separate from #350, which fixed the 32-bit float backends.

## What happens

`aorsf_tree_info_full()` (`R/model-aorsf.R:58-62`) folds the forest's centering and scaling into the split coefficients:

```r
coefs <- as.numeric(cv / sdv)
threshold <- cutpoint[i] + sum(cv * mu / sdv)
```

so the generated formula compares `sum(cv / sdv * x)` against `cutpoint + sum(cv * mu / sdv)`, where aorsf itself compares `sum(cv * (x - mu) / sdv)` against `cutpoint`. Algebraically identical, numerically not: a different sequence of roundings, disagreeing in the last bit.

That would normally be harmless. It is not harmless here, because **aorsf's cutpoints are observed linear-combination values**, so every training row lands exactly on one of them, and a last-bit difference sends it down the other branch.

## Measured

A 25-tree regression forest on 300 rows, 4 numeric predictors:

- 339,600 split comparisons over the training rows, of which **650 are exact ties** and **338 flip branch**
- **182 of 300 training rows** get a different prediction from `tidypredict_fit()` than from `predict()`, max abs diff **0.25**

Predicting on genuinely new data is fine, which is why the suite is green: `tests/testthat/test-model-aorsf.R` jitters `mtcars` for exactly this reason, and its header comment records the behaviour as known. This issue is to quantify it and to fix it rather than avoid it.

## What is not the answer

Two things I checked, so the next person does not repeat them:

- Emitting the unfolded form `sum(cv * (x - mu) / sdv) <= cutpoint` term by term **improves but does not fix** it: 182 rows differing becomes 165. So this grouping is still not aorsf's own order of operations.
- The operator direction is not the issue. `<=` is right; `<` is much worse (271 of 300 differ).

Since the folded and the term-by-term centered forms are both wrong, and only in the last bit, fixing this needs aorsf's actual C++ traversal arithmetic (the order it accumulates the linear combination, and whether it standardizes the row first or scales the coefficients) rather than another guess from R. Whatever form is chosen has to reproduce that sequence exactly for the exact ties to land correctly.

Note also that the parsed/saved path builds these expressions separately, so both need the same treatment, and the boundary of a change here is the parsed-model format: carrying centers and scales separately means a model parsed by an older version has folded coefficients and no centers.

title: bart with default `ntree` produces a formula R cannot evaluate
description:
`R/model-bart.R:19-26` uses `reduce_addition()`, which builds a left-deep `+` chain over `n_draws * ntree` trees. With dbarts' default `ntree = 200` and `ndpost = 50` that is 10,000 nested calls:

```
n trees total: 10000
tidypredict_fit(): built ok
eval_tidy():       "evaluation nested too deeply: infinite recursion / options(expressions=)?"
```

Real defaults (`ntree = 200`, `ndpost = 1000`) give 200,000 terms. This is a build-time wall rather than a wrong number, but it means the parser does not work on a default `bart()` fit at all.

The whole bart test file uses `ntree = 1..10` and `ndpost = 1..8`, which is why this has never surfaced.

**Fix.** Sum with a balanced divide-and-conquer reduction so nesting depth is `log2(n)` rather than `n`. Making `reduce_addition()` itself balanced would be the better fix, since it also helps xgboost, ranger and aorsf on large ensembles.

Add a test at or near dbarts' defaults that actually evaluates the formula.

title: randomForest: a stump in the forest aborts with "argument of length 0"
description:
Found by the degenerate-fits battery.

`randomForest` regression models abort with a base-R error whenever any tree in the forest is a stump, i.e. has a single root node and no split:

```r
set.seed(1)
d <- data.frame(x1 = rnorm(120), x2 = runif(120))
d$y <- 3   # constant outcome

m <- randomForest::randomForest(y ~ x1 + x2, data = d, ntree = 10)
tidypredict_fit(m)
#> Error in `map()`:
#> i In index: 1.
#> Caused by error in `1:nrow(tree)`:
#> ! argument of length 0
```

The same error appears for a zero-variance predictor, which is the more realistic route in:

```r
d2 <- data.frame(x1 = rnorm(120), xconst = 1)
d2$y <- 2 * d2$x1 + rnorm(120, sd = 0.3)
m2 <- randomForest::randomForest(y ~ x1 + xconst, data = d2, ntree = 10)
tidypredict_fit(m2)
#> ! argument of length 0     (in index: 2, i.e. a particular tree)
```

`predict()` handles both fine, returning the constant in the first case and the ordinary fitted values in the second. So this is a tidypredict-side crash, not a modelling limitation.

`getTree()` returns a zero-row frame for a stump, and `1:nrow(tree)` on that gives `1:0`, which is where the error comes from. The fix is to emit the tree's single prediction rather than walking its (empty) node table, the same shape of guard `.build_case_when_tree()` already has.

Related but distinct from #310, which is about the stump path in `R/tree.R`; this one is in the randomForest parser and fires before that code is reached.

Whichever fix lands, a regression test with a stump-producing fit would be worth having: the whole randomForest test file uses well-conditioned data, which is why this has never surfaced.

title: `lda` errors when the outcome factor has an unused level
description:
`R/model-lda.R:15` does `classes <- model$lev`, which keeps **all** factor levels. MASS drops empty groups, so `model$prior`, `model$means` and `predict()`'s posterior cover only the observed ones, and `lapply(seq_along(classes), ...)` then indexes `intercepts[[4]]`:

```
y levels c("a","b","c","zzz"), zzz unused
m$lev = a b c zzz ; names(m$prior) = a b c ; ncol(predict()$posterior) = 3
tidypredict_fit(m) -> Error: subscript out of bounds
```

**Fix.** `classes <- names(model$prior)` (equivalently `rownames(model$means)`).

`qda` is unaffected because MASS refuses to fit, and `fda` already uses `rownames(model$means)` and was verified correct on the same data — so this is genuinely lda-only.

title: ksvm: single-column model matrices lose all terms, and one-column scaling is not undone
description:
Two faults with the same root cause: kernlab drops names when a matrix or attribute vector has exactly one column, and `R/model-ksvm.R` indexes by name.

**Terms silently dropped for a single-column model matrix** (`:56-57`, `:129`). `names(weights) <- colnames(sv)`, but kernlab leaves `colnames(xmatrix(model)[[1]])` `NULL` for one column. `names(weights)` is then `NULL`, so `for (feature in names(linear))` iterates **zero times** and the parsed model contains only the intercept:

```
ksvm(mpg ~ wt, kernel = "vanilladot", type = "eps-svr")
tidypredict_fit() -> 19.90148            # a bare constant
max abs diff = 10.97 ; tidypredict_test()$alert = TRUE
same with scaled = FALSE                 -> 23.29
ksvm(Species ~ Sepal.Length, ...) 2-class probability -> 0.55
```

Fix: fall back to a real feature name when `colnames(sv)` is `NULL` (e.g. the non-response entries of `attr(model@terms, "dataClasses")` when `ncol(sv)` matches), and hard-error rather than emit a term-free model if names still cannot be recovered.

**Scaling not undone when exactly one column was scaled** (`:63-74`). `kernlab::scaling(model)$x.scale[["scaled:center"]]` and `[["scaled:scale"]]` are **unnamed** whenever only one column is scaled, because kernlab builds them from `attributes(x[, scaled])`, which drops to a plain vector. The loop tests `nm %in% names(scales)`, which is then never `TRUE`, so weights and intercept stay on the scaled scale. This hits any fit with one numeric predictor plus factor predictors, since dummy columns are not scaled:

```
mpg ~ wt + hp + gear (the existing test, 2 numeric) -> 3.553e-15  ok
mpg ~ wt + gear      (1 numeric + factor)           -> 14.59      alert = TRUE
Sepal.Length ~ Sepal.Width + Species                -> 1.413
y ~ x + g, C-svc probabilities                      -> 0.4015
```

Fix: index positionally using `kernlab::scaling(model)$scaled`, a logical vector aligned with the model-matrix columns:

```r
idx <- which(rep_len(kernlab::scaling(model)$scaled, length(weights)))
for (j in seq_along(idx)) {
  k <- idx[[j]]
  linear[[k]] <- weights[[k]] / scales[[j]]
  intercept   <- intercept - weights[[k]] * centers[[j]] / scales[[j]]
}
```

`test-model-ksvm.R:31` uses two numeric predictors, which is exactly why both bugs pass today. New tests should use one numeric predictor, and one numeric plus a factor.

Also in this file: `:158` passes `call. = FALSE` to `cli::cli_abort()`, which takes `call`, not `call.` — the dotted name is swallowed by `...`.

title: Matrix-interface `nnet()` fits emit a formula full of `NULL`
description:
`R/model-nnet.R:121-125`:

```r
vars <- names(attr(model$terms, "dataClasses")) %||% model$coefnames
```

`nnet.default()` never sets `$coefnames` (there is no such assignment in `nnet:::nnet.default`) and `$terms` is `NULL`, so `vars` is `NULL`, `inputs` is empty, and the input-unit expressions come out as `NULL`:

```r
m <- nnet(as.matrix(mtcars[, c("wt","hp")]), mtcars$mpg, size = 2, linout = TRUE)
tidypredict_fit(m)
#> 6.2747 + case_when(-0.3510 + NULL * 0.4562 + NULL * 5.4119 < -15 ~ 0, ...
```

It evaluates to nothing rather than aborting. Note the `%||% model$coefnames` fallback is dead code as written, since `$coefnames` is never populated for these fits.

**Fix.** Abort with a clear message when both `model$terms` and `model$coefnames` are absent, pointing the user at the formula interface. Taking names from `dimnames(model$residuals)` would be an alternative if matrix fits should be supported.

title: glm probit link diverges from predict() by 1.4e-4, and the approximation is undocumented
description:
Found by the ignored-fit-options battery.

## What happens

`apply_inverse_link()` (`R/model-lm.R:52`) writes the probit inverse link as the Bowling et al. logistic approximation to the normal CDF:

```r
"probit" = expr(1 / (1 + exp(-0.07056 * (!!f)^3 - 1.5976 * (!!f))))
```

Measured against `predict(type = "response")` on a `glm(family = binomial(link = "probit"))`: **max abs diff 1.41e-4**, which matches the approximation's stated ~0.014% error. So the code is doing what it means to do; this issue is about whether it should, and about the fact that nothing says so.

## Why it is worth raising

Every other link in that `switch()` is exact. A user comparing `tidypredict_fit()` against `predict()` for a probit model sees a disagreement four orders of magnitude larger than the ~1e-15 every other member of the linear family delivers, with nothing in the documentation to explain it. `grep -r probit` over the vignettes, man pages and README turns up exactly one hit, in `bart.Rmd`, about a different model's classification.

The reason for the approximation is presumably SQL: no SQL backend has a normal CDF, so `pnorm()` cannot be translated. That trade is defensible, but it is invisible.

## Options

1. **Document it** and leave the behaviour alone, in the same style as the naive Bayes divergence in #300. Cheapest, and keeps one expression serving both backends.
2. **Emit `pnorm()` for the R path and keep the approximation for SQL.** Exact where it can be, approximate only where it must be. Costs a branch between the two paths, which the package does not currently have for links.
3. Leave as is, undocumented. Not recommended: it looks like a bug to anyone who checks.

My inclination is option 1, possibly with 2 later, but this is a design call rather than something to fix unilaterally.

Worth noting `tidypredict_test()`'s default threshold would not flag this either, so a user following the documented verification workflow gets a pass on a model that is measurably off.

title: h2o: every non-GBM algorithm is silently treated as a GBM
description:
`R/model-h2o.R:74-114` carries the comment "Only GBM models are supported", but dispatch is on `H2ORegressionModel` / `H2OBinomialModel` / `H2OMultinomialModel`, and **every** H2O algorithm produces one of those classes. Nothing checks `model@algorithm`; only rulefit is special-cased.

- `h2o.randomForest` regression (ntrees = 5): `predict()[1] = 21.22` vs tidypredict `106.1`, **max abs diff 127.5**. DRF *averages* tree predictions where the code sums them — `max(abs(base - te/5)) = 7.6e-7`, i.e. off by exactly `ntrees`.
- DRF binomial: `predict()` probabilities `1, 1, 0.6` vs tidypredict `0.5, 0.5, 0.881`. DRF classification uses vote proportions, not `logistic(sum)`.
- GLM and DeepLearning: `h2o_n_trees()` returns `NULL`, so `seq_len(NULL)` raises the cryptic "argument must be coercible to non-negative integer".

**Fix.** In all three `tidypredict_fit.H2O*` methods, after the rulefit branch:

```r
if (!identical(model@algorithm, "gbm")) {
  cli::cli_abort("tidypredict only supports h2o GBM models, not {.val {model@algorithm}}.")
}
```

Supporting DRF properly (`expr_division(sum, n_trees)` for regression, per-class vote averaging for classification) would be a reasonable follow-up.

title: xgboost: reloaded boosters error, or return raw logits labelled as probabilities
description:
`R/model-xgboost.R:72,124,239,384-397` discriminate old vs new xgboost API with `is.null(attr(model, "param"))`. That attribute is set by `xgb.train()` and **not** by `xgb.load()`, so a saved-and-reloaded booster takes the legacy branch and calls `xgb.model.dt.tree(text = ...)` — an argument xgboost 3.x has removed:

```
xgb loaded attr param NULL? TRUE   params$objective: NULL
Warning: Parameter(s) have been removed from this function: text.
ERROR: argument "model" is missing, with no default
```

Worse, when that branch is bypassed, `params$objective` is `NULL`, so `apply_xgb_objective()` (`:299-309`) only **warns** and returns the raw margin:

```
maxdiff vs predict (probabilities): 1.360145
got:      1.9261 1.9261 1.9261 -1.1018
expected: 0.7577 0.7577 0.7577  0.1315
```

The user gets logits presented as probabilities, behind a warning that misdescribes the cause ("If the objective is a custom function…").

**Fix.**

1. Stop using `attr(model, "param")` as the discriminator. `xgb.model.dt.tree(model = ...)` and `xgb.get.num.boosted.rounds()` work for both trained and loaded 3.x boosters; gate on the xgboost version instead.
2. Recover the objective from the saved JSON in `get_xgb_json_params()`, which already reads that file. The field is confirmed present — `objective":{"name":"binary:logistic","reg_loss_param":...` — so a regex alongside the existing `base_score` extraction is enough.

Note that fixing (1) must not un-mask a latent bug in the legacy path: `get_xgb_trees_df()` does `merge(trees, feature_names_tbl, by = "Feature")` at `:408` and **never restores the original row order**, unlike `get_xgb_trees_character()` which saves it at `:96` and restores at `:108-111`. `merge()` sorts by `Feature`, and `:414-420` then converts node IDs to row *positions* assuming row `i` is node `i-1`. Please fix both together.

Add an `xgb.save()` / `xgb.load()` round-trip test.

title: glmnet: `offset=` is silently dropped
description:
`R/model-glmnet.R:31-49` ignores `model$offset`, which is a reliable logical flag (`TRUE`/`FALSE`) on the fitted object.

```r
g <- glmnet(x, mtcars$cyl, family = "poisson", lambda = .05, offset = mtcars$am)
tidypredict_fit(g)   #> exp(0.0510 + wt*0.2644 + ...)     # no offset
```

**Max abs diff 7.474** against `predict(g, x, newoffset = mtcars$am, type = "response")`.

glmnet does not store the offset *values* on the object, only the flag, so the prediction cannot be reconstructed. The correct action is to abort:

```r
if (isTRUE(model$offset)) {
  cli::cli_abort("Models fit with {.arg offset} are not supported.")
}
```

title: ranger: probability and survival forests bypass the classification guard
description:
`R/model-ranger.R:6-10` and `:65-69` test `first_tree$prediction[...]` to detect classification. Probability and survival forests have **no** `prediction` column, so `NULL[...]` is `NULL`, `is.character(NULL)` is `FALSE`, and the guard passes.

`tidypredict_fit()` then emits `case_when(x1 <= 0.0066 ~ NULL, .default = NULL)`, and `parse_model()` returns a parsed model with no predictions and no error at all. Evaluation eventually fails with an unrelated vctrs error (`..1 (right) must be a vector, not NULL`), which gives the user nothing to work with.

**Fix.** Guard on `model$treeType`, which is `"Classification"`, `"Probability estimation"` or `"Survival"`, or equivalently on `is.null(first_tree$prediction)`. Probability forests should be routed to the existing `.extract_ranger_classprob()` message rather than a generic abort.

title: mboost: `mstop` reduction after fitting is ignored
description:
`R/model-mboost.R:26-51`. `mboost_components()` pulls `ens` out of the predict closure and uses all of it. Subsetting a model — `model[m]`, which is the standard `cvrisk()` → `model[mstop(cv)]` workflow — sets `mstop` in that same environment but leaves `ens` at full length.

```r
f <- blackboost(mpg ~ wt + hp, mtcars, control = boost_control(mstop = 100))
f[30]
mstop(f)      # 30
length(ens)   # 100
max abs diff vs predict() = 0.8409312      (0 before subsetting)
```

**Fix.**

```r
ens <- ens[seq_len(get("mstop", envir = e))]
```

`mstop` is already in the same environment as `ens` (verified via `ls()`), and increasing `mstop` grows `ens`, so truncation is always the right operation.

Add a test that subsets a fitted model before parsing.

title: naive Bayes: NA handling and `threshold` diverge from both references
description:
- [ ] **Missing values and unseen factor levels propagate `NA` instead of being skipped.** `R/model-naivebayes.R:66-68` and the numeric/poisson/logical branches. Both references **skip** a feature whose value is missing — klaR: `if (is.na(nd)) return(rep(1, length(apriori)))`; naivebayes: `p[is.na(p)] <- 1` — and `klaR::predict.NaiveBayes()` coerces unseen factor levels to `NA`, which takes that same skip path.
  ```
  row x=NA, g="u"     klaR: 0.3684 0.3158 0.3158   tidypredict: NA NA NA
  row x=1,  g=NA      klaR: 0.5794 0.3753 0.0453   tidypredict: NA NA NA
  row x=1,  g="zzz"   klaR: 0.5794 0.3753 0.0453   tidypredict: NA NA NA
  ```
  naivebayes gives the same three finite rows. **The code comment claiming this "matches the `NA` that `predict.NaiveBayes()` returns for them" is factually wrong** and should be corrected along with the behaviour. Fix: emit `.default = 0` (a log-density of 0 is a density of 1) for the categorical `case_when()`, and wrap numeric/poisson/logical terms in `coalesce(..., 0)`.

- [ ] **`threshold` is applied at parse time only, not to evaluated densities.** `:100-126`, `:160-215`. Both references clamp the *evaluated* density (`prob[prob == 0] <- threshold` in klaR, `p[p <= eps] <- threshold` in naivebayes), including Gaussian and Poisson densities; tidypredict bakes the clamp into the fitted categorical tables only.
  ```
  klaR::NaiveBayes(Species ~ ., iris), x = (10, 2, 8, 3)
  klaR:        setosa 0             versicolor 2.931152e-29  virginica 1
  tidypredict: setosa 6.254739e-211 versicolor 1.995139e-40  virginica 1
  ```
  Arguably tidypredict is the more faithful *statistics* here, but it is not what the reference returns, and the parsed model already carries `general$threshold`, so the current half-application is inconsistent either way. Either replicate the clamp (`pmax(offset - (x-mean)^2/scale, log(0.001))`) or document the divergence explicitly.

- [ ] **Uninformative error when a class has fewer than 2 observations.** `:190`: `if (sd <= 0)` on an `NA` sd raises "missing value where TRUE/FALSE needed". Reproduced with a 1-observation class and with an empty outcome level (naivebayes fits both; `predict()` returns `NA` probabilities). Fix: `if (is.na(sd) || sd <= 0)` to reproduce the reference's `NA`, or abort naming the class.

title: NA in a predictor is silently mispredicted in every tree model
description:
`R/tree-nested.R:34-37` states that "results will be NA for those rows". That is not what happens. `build_nested_node()` emits `case_when(cond ~ left, .default = right)`, and dplyr sends `NA` conditions to `.default`, so every row with a missing predictor gets a confident, arbitrary prediction down the right branch:

```r
rlang::eval_tidy(
  rlang::expr(dplyr::case_when(x <= 5 ~ 10, .default = 20)),
  data.frame(x = NA_real_)
)
#> 20     (not NA)
```

The same applies to `%in%` (`NA %in% c("a")` is `FALSE` → right branch) and to the flat form at `R/tree.R:64-69`. Confirmed across the model families:

- `partykit::ctree(mpg ~ wt + cyl, mtcars)` with `wt = NA`: partykit `15.1`, tidypredict `20.75`.
- rpart with 30/300 rows at `x1 = NA`: **30/30 rows mismatch**, max abs diff 3.669404 at `usesurrogate = 2` (the default) and 2.306808 at `usesurrogate = 0`.
- bart: `predict() = 0.612` vs tidypredict `3.264`.
- C5.0 on iris with 3 NAs: 1/150 wrong class. (C5.0 itself splits the case fractionally down all branches via `FollowAllBranches`.)

**The rpart half of this is worse, because the fix is already half-written and then discarded.** `rpart_tree_info_full()` carefully extracts `surrogates` (`R/model-rpart.R:78-90`), `majority_left` (`:92-97`) and `use_surrogates` (`:127`), but **no generator ever reads them**: `build_nested_node()` uses only `split_info$primary` (`R/tree-nested.R:88`), and grep confirms `majority_left` and `surrogates` appear nowhere outside the parsers. The comments at `R/model-rpart.R:22-25` and the claim at `vignettes/rpart.Rmd:44` that tidypredict "handles … surrogate splits" do not hold.

**Fix, in order of preference:**

1. Implement surrogates in `build_nested_split_condition()`: left iff `!is.na(primary) & primary_left`, else the first non-NA surrogate, else `majority_left`. This makes rpart match `predict()` and is what the parsed model is already carrying data for.
2. For the general case, wrap each tree so that NA in any split variable yields `NA_real_`. Note that guarding the condition alone (`!is.na(col) & col <= val`) does **not** fix this — it just moves NA to the right branch deliberately.
Whichever route is taken, `R/tree-nested.R:34-37`, `R/model-rpart.R:22-25` and `vignettes/rpart.Rmd:44` need to end up describing what the code actually does — option 1 makes the rpart claim true, option 2 makes the "results will be NA" claim true, and if the surrogate extraction stays unused it should be deleted.

title: C5.0: four correctness bugs (float32 cuts, `[ordered]`, boosted confidence, leaf argmax)
description:
Four independent faults in `R/model-C5.0.R`. Applying all four takes a 25-dataset × trials {1,2,3,5,10} × rules {T,F} battery from **124 of 150 configurations failing to 0 of 75**, so they are best fixed together.

- [ ] **Continuous cuts are compared as doubles; C5.0 compares in float32.** `:111` (`val = as.numeric(attrs$cut)`) and `:379`. C50 is built with `PREC 7` and `ContValue = float` (`defns.h`), writes cuts as `%.8g`, and `PredictInterpolate()` compares single-precision values. **124/150 configurations disagreed** with `predict()` (1–4 rows per 200). The class-probability path is hit much harder: off by up to **0.93 absolute** on 8 of 10 datasets. Fix: apply `f32_split_boundary(as.numeric(attrs$cut), side = "upper")`, the helper Cubist already uses. That alone drops tree models to 19/150, rule-based models to **0**, and makes class probabilities match `predict(type = "prob")` to ≤2e-8.

- [ ] **The `[ordered]` marker is never stripped from the level list.** `c50_attr_levels()`, `:38-52`. C50 writes an ordered predictor in `model$names` as `g: [ordered]p,q.`, so lines 48-49 return `c("[ordered]p", "q")` and the first level of every ordered predictor becomes an unmatchable string in a `type="1"` multiway split. **88 of 400 rows wrong (22%), silently.** Fix: drop a leading `[ordered]` after the colon before `strsplit(..., ",")`, and handle `[label]`, `[ignore]` and `discrete N` defensively while there.

- [ ] **Boosted trials use the wrong per-trial confidence.** `:86-90` uses the Laplace ratio `(freq+1)/(n+2)`. `PredictBoostClassify()` does `Vote[Best] += Confidence`, where `Confidence` comes from `PredictTreeClassify()` as `(n_leaf * p_c + prior_c)/(n_leaf + 1)` — i.e. `(freq[best] + prior[best])/(sum(freq) + 1)`, with `prior` being *that trial's own* root `ClassDist/Cases`. Laplace leaves **13 of 75** boosted configurations wrong; the blended value gives **0 of 75**. Note `c50_priors()` (`:291`) only reads the first tree's root, so this needs per-trial root frequencies.

- [ ] **A leaf's class should be the argmax of its `freq`, not the stored `class=` attribute.** `FindLeafGen` accumulates `ClassDist[c]/Cases` and `SelectClassGen()` starts from `Default` (= `Pruned[0]->Leaf`, the first tree's root class), replacing only on a strict `>`. Ties therefore go to the default class, not the stored leaf label. Repro (seed 24): leaf `class="c1" freq="1,1,0,0"`, `predict()` returns `c2` (its probabilities `0.375/0.4667/0.12/0.0383` reproduce exactly as `(freq+prior)/(n+1)`), tidypredict returns `c1`.

Two smaller related items, fine to fold in or split out:

- Boosted vote ties should break on the default class, not the first level (`c50_boosted_case_when()`, `:351-357`); the rules path already does this at `:480`.
- Predictor level names containing `,` or `:` abort with `subscript out of bounds` from `attr_levels[[attrs$att]]` (`:119-123`). C50 does not escape them either, so the model is already invalid — but a clear error beats a subscript error. The comment at `:36-37` claiming C50 escapes them is wrong.

title: `expr_softmax()` overflows to `NaN`
description:
`R/misc.R:62-69` emits `exp(s_k) / sum(exp(s_j))` with no max-subtraction. Every reference implementation subtracts the row maximum first (`MASS:::predict.lda` and `.qda`, `sda:::predict.sda`, `naivebayes`), so where they return a valid distribution tidypredict returns `NaN` from `0/0`:

```
qda(Species ~ ., iris), x = (100,100,100,100)      MASS: 0 0 1   tidypredict: NaN NaN NaN
lda(Species ~ ., iris), x = (1e3,-1e3,1e3,-1e3)    MASS: 0 1 0   tidypredict: 0 NaN 0
klaR NaiveBayes(Species ~ ., iris), x = (12,2,9,3)              -> NaN NaN NaN
synthetic scores (800, 0, -800)                                 -> NaN 0 0
```

This is shared machinery, so it reaches **lda, qda, sda, sparsediscrim, fda, naive_bayes, plsda, multinom and multiclass glmnet**.

**Fix.** Build the row maximum once and subtract it inside the generated expression:

```r
mx <- pmax(s_1, ..., s_K)
exp(s_k - mx) / sum(exp(s_j - mx))
```

`pmax()` translates to `GREATEST()` on the usual SQL backends, so this stays database-safe. If for some reason it cannot be done, the limitation should at least be recorded in a comment and in the docs.

title: lda, qda and fda silently mis-parse an ordered factor
description:
`MASS::lda()`, `MASS::qda()` and `mda::fda()` all call `acceptable_formula()`, which routes to `acceptable_lm()`, whose contrast check reads `model$contrasts`. None of the three records that field, so the check is a no-op and an unsupported contrast reaches the parser.

An ordered factor, which R fits with `contr.poly` by default, expands into columns named `f.L`, `f.Q` and `f.C`. `parse_label_lm()` recovers `".L"` as the level, and emits `ifelse(f == ".L", ...)`, which no row ever matches. The term is silently dropped rather than erroring, so the posteriors come out wrong with no complaint:

```r
set.seed(1)
n <- 200
f <- factor(sample(c("a", "b", "c", "d"), n, TRUE), ordered = TRUE)
d <- data.frame(x = rnorm(n), z = rnorm(n), f = f)
d$y <- rnorm(n) + as.numeric(d$f) + 0.5 * d$x
d$cls <- factor(ifelse(d$y > median(d$y), "hi", "lo"))

m <- MASS::lda(cls ~ x + z + f, data = d)
fit <- tidypredict_fit(m)
max(abs(sapply(fit, \(f) rlang::eval_tidy(f, d)) - predict(m, d)$posterior))
#> 0.625
```

Max absolute difference against each package's own `predict()`, on the same data:

| class | unordered factor | ordered factor |
|---|---|---|
| `MASS::lda` | 2.2e-16 | **0.625** |
| `MASS::qda` | 1.2e-15 | **0.848** |
| `mda::fda` | 3.3e-16 | **0.630** |

`lm`, `glm`, `rq`, `nnet` and `multinom` all abort cleanly on the same data, because they do record `contrasts`.

**Fix direction.** #323 added `acceptable_contrasts(columns, vars, xlevels)` in `R/acceptable.R` for exactly this situation, where a model does not record its contrasts. It checks that every column a factor expanded into is named after one of that factor's levels. `lda` and `qda` both store `xlevels` and expose the expanded names as `colnames(model$means)`; `fda` needs its equivalent located.

Also worth covering while there: a global `options(contrasts = c("contr.sum", "contr.poly"))` produces columns `f1`, `f2`, `f3` on an *unordered* factor, which is the same fault and equally silent.

Found by sweeping an ordered factor across every supported regression and discriminant class, while fixing #323. `kernlab::ksvm` and the four `sparsediscrim` classes were swept at the same time and are unaffected. `xrf::xrf()` refuses to fit an ordered factor upstream, in `correct_xgb_sparse_categoricals()`, so it never reaches tidypredict.

title: earth: an ordered factor bypasses the contrast guard and emits a nonsense formula
description:
`R/model-earth.R` never calls `acceptable_formula()`, so an ordered factor (which R fits with `contr.poly` by default) is parsed as if its polynomial contrast values were the column itself. `tidypredict_fit()` returns without complaint and emits comparisons of the factor column against contrast values:

```r
set.seed(1)
n <- 200
f <- factor(sample(c("a", "b", "c", "d"), n, TRUE), ordered = TRUE)
d <- data.frame(x = rnorm(n), z = rnorm(n), f = f)
d$y <- rnorm(n) + as.numeric(d$f) + 0.5 * d$x

tidypredict_fit(earth::earth(y ~ x + z + f, data = d))
#> 2.4002144963064 + (ifelse(f < -0.223606797749979, -0.223606797749979 -
#>     f, 0) * -2.52778983361519) + (ifelse(x < 0.105802367893711,
#>     0.105802367893711 - x, 0) * -0.799801359371858) + (ifelse(f >
#>     -0.223606797749979, f - -0.223606797749979, 0) * 1.82087313337739)
```

`-0.2236` is the `contr.poly` linear-contrast value, not a level of `f`. Evaluating this fails with `missing value where TRUE/FALSE needed`.

Every other model in the linear family aborts cleanly on the same data, because they route through `acceptable_formula()`:

```r
tidypredict_fit(lm(y ~ x + z + f, d))
#> Error: The treatment contrast is the only one supported at this time.
#>        Field(s) with an invalid contrast are: contr.poly.
```

`lm`, `glm`, `rq` and `nnet` all give that message. earth should do the same rather than emitting a formula that cannot be evaluated. An unordered factor on the same data is fine (max abs diff 4.4e-16), so this is specific to the contrast, not to factors generally.

This is adjacent to but distinct from #291: there the contrast check is too permissive, here it is not reached at all.

Found by sweeping an ordered factor across every supported regression class.

title: catboost: `set_catboost_categories()` fails for most factor level counts
description:
`identify_catboost_hashes()` (`R/model-catboost.R:259-283`) discovers category hashes by training probe models, but records a mapping only when a probe's `features_info` happens to contain exactly one hash, and `fill_catboost_hash_mapping()` resolves only a single leftover.

Sweeping 8 seeds × 2–6 levels, **30 of 40 models were left unmapped**, failing later in `build_nested_catboost_categorical()` with "No category mapping found for hash …". Only 3-level factors work reliably: k=2 succeeded 2/8; k=4, 5 and 6 failed 8/8.

**Every categorical test in `test-model-catboost.R` uses exactly three levels** (`:58`, `:1335`, `:1429`, …), which is why the suite is green. This also breaks `tidypredict_fit_catboost_parsnip()` and therefore bonsai, which route through the same function.

Secondary risk: `:277` does `mapping[[hash_str]] <- cat` unconditionally, so two probes yielding the same hash would silently produce a **wrong** category rather than an error. Not observed, but reachable.

**Fix direction.** Reading the hash from the depth-1 probe's `oblivious_trees[[1]]$splits[[1]]$value` instead of `features_info$…$values` is more robust, though still incomplete for k ∈ {2,3,6} in testing. Regardless of the discovery strategy, `set_catboost_categories()` should **abort as soon as any hash is unmapped** rather than deferring the failure to fit time.

Tests should cover 2, 4, 5 and 6 levels.

title: cubist: the per-rule extrapolation clamp is never applied
description:
Cubist clamps each rule's linear-model output to that rule's own observed target range, widened by `extrapolation` percent: `[lo - p*(hi-lo), hi + p*(hi-lo)]` with `p = extrapolation/100` (default 100). `R/model-cubist.R:121-141` emits the raw linear model.

Single-rule model, `Rule 1: [400 cases, mean 1.0034686, range 0.01683731 to 1.92487]`, so the upper limit is `1.92487 + 1*(1.92487-0.01683731) = 3.832903`:

```
newdata a=b=50 :  predict() = 3.832903   tidypredict =  99.99452   (diff 96.2)
newdata a=b=-50:  predict() = 0.000000   tidypredict = -100.0055
```

`predict()` returns the clamp bound exactly. This is also visible in-sample: with `cubistControl(extrapolation = 0)` the max abs diff is **0.156 on the training data itself**, and even at the default the clamp bites on 1/800 training rows.

Worth noting: **this bug is why cubist currently looks like a float32-noise case.** The residual ~1e-6 on mtcars/iris that reads as coefficient rounding is actually the missing clamp.

**Fix.** Parse `range <lo> to <hi>` per rule out of `model$output` (the `[n cases, mean m, range lo to hi]` header), store `lo`/`hi` and `extrapolation` in the parsed model, and wrap each rule's prediction in

```r
pmin(pmax(pred, lo - p * (hi - lo)), hi + p * (hi - lo))
```

Note this changes the parsed-model format. `parse_model.cubist()` emits `version = 3` (`R/model-cubist.R:105`), and cubist has been supported since tidypredict 0.4.0 (#36), so saved cubist parsed models exist in the wild and will not carry the new `lo`/`hi`/`extrapolation` fields. Decide explicitly what `tidypredict_fit()` should do with one — erroring with a clear message is better than silently omitting the clamp, since omitting it is the current bug. This needs a version bump and a backwards-compat fixture; note there is currently no generator script for the existing `cubist-v2-regression.rds` fixture, so it cannot be regenerated as things stand.

title: cubist: a factor predictor produces an unevaluable formula
description:
A `Cubist::cubist()` model fitted with a factor predictor produces a formula that R cannot evaluate. The split condition keeps the quoted column name and gets no threshold:

```r
set.seed(1)
n <- 120
df <- data.frame(
  y = rnorm(n),
  x = rnorm(n),
  f = factor(sample(c("a", "b", "c", "d"), n, TRUE))
)
df$y <- df$y + as.numeric(df$f) + 0.5 * df$x

mf <- model.frame(y ~ x + f, df)
model <- Cubist::cubist(x = mf[, -1, drop = FALSE], y = mf[[1]])

tidypredict_fit(model)
#> (ifelse(`"f"` <= NA_real_, 1.384984 + x * 0.58, 0) + ifelse(`"f"` <=
#>     NA_real_, 3.7233071 + x * 0.55, 0))/((`"f"` <= NA_real_) +
#>     (`"f"` <= NA_real_))

rlang::eval_tidy(tidypredict_fit(model), df)
#> Error: object '"f"' not found
```

Two things go wrong in the same place: the column name is carried through with its surrounding quotes, so it is backtick-quoted into a name that does not exist, and the categorical split value never becomes a threshold, so it is `NA_real_`. Cubist writes categorical rules as `f in {a, b}` style conditions rather than as a numeric cut, and the parser appears to read them with the numeric path.

Found by sweeping a 4-level unordered factor across every supported regression class rather than one model at a time. The other 15 classes in that sweep either matched their own `predict()` to ~1e-15 or failed in a way already tracked (#282 randomForest, #283 ranger); this one has no existing issue. #285 and #286 are about the extrapolation clamp and committee assignment and do not cover it.

Every categorical test in `test-model-cubist.R` goes through the x/y interface with numeric predictors only, which is why the suite is green.

title: partykit: `right`, multiway splits, and ordered factors
description:
Three faults in `R/model-partykit.R`.

- [ ] **`partysplit$right` is ignored.** `:85` reads only `breaks`; nothing reads `node$split$right`, and `build_nested_split_condition()` always emits `<=` (`R/tree-nested.R:120`). With `right = FALSE` the left branch is `x < break`. Hand-built `party` with `partysplit(1L, breaks = 3, right = FALSE)`, `x = 1:6`:
  ```
  partykit   : 15 15 45 45 45 45
  tidypredict: 15 15 15 45 45 45     max abs diff = 30
  ```
  `partykit::as.party.rpart()` produces `right = FALSE` splits (confirmed), so this is reachable from real objects — it escapes notice there only because rpart cut points are midpoints that never coincide with data values. Fix: carry `right` into the split info and set `strict = !right`. The mechanism already exists at `R/tree-nested.R:114-117` for rpart.

- [ ] **Multiway splits silently collapse to two branches.** `:87-89` keeps only `kids[[1]]` and `kids[[2]]`; `:85` assigns a length-`k` `breaks` into a length-1 slot; `:147` treats only `index == 1` as left.
  ```
  ctree(y ~ f, ctree_control(multiway = TRUE))   # 4 kids at root
  max abs diff = 2.928334
  3-way numeric split (breaks = c(-0.5, 0.5)):
    Warning: number of items to replace is not a multiple of replacement length
    max abs diff = 1.163571
  ```
  Fix: abort when `length(kids) > 2` or `length(breaks) > 1`, or generalize the generator to an n-way `case_when` with one clause per kid — which is the natural representation and probably the better end state.

- [ ] **Ordered-factor predictors error.** `:132` does `map_chr(model$data, class)`, but `class()` of an ordered factor is `c("ordered","factor")`:
  ```
  ctree(y ~ x1 + o)
  #> Error in map_chr(model$data, class): Result must be length 1, not 2.
  ```
  The `== "factor"` test at `:143` would also misclassify ordered factors as continuous even without the length error. Fix: `vapply(model$data, function(x) class(x)[[1]], character(1))` and test `is.factor()`; then handle the ordered case, since partykit splits ordered factors via `breaks` on level codes and needs `match(x, levels)` rather than a comparison against the factor.

---

# Priority 2 — wrong results in narrower configurations, and errors

title: ranger factor splits are wrong in all three `respect.unordered.factors` modes
description:
`R/model-ranger.R:31-40` and `:112` never interpret `treeInfo()$splitval` according to the fit's `respect.unordered.factors` mode; the value is always compared with `<=` against the factor column itself.

```
respect.unordered.factors = "ignore"     max abs diff = 3.496109
                            "order"      max abs diff = 6.169886
                            "partition"  max abs diff = 5.189210
ordered-factor predictor                 max abs diff = 4.418488
.extract_ranger_classprob with a factor  max probability error = 0.873481
```

The metadata needed is already on the object: `model$forest$covariate.levels` (per independent variable) and `model$forest$is.ordered`. Both decodings below were verified to give **max abs diff 0** against `ranger::predict()` in a one-tree repro:

- `is.ordered[j] == TRUE` (covers both `"ignore"` and `"order"`): left iff `match(as.character(x), covariate.levels[[j]]) <= splitval`, i.e. `x %in% covariate.levels[[j]][seq_len(floor(splitval))]`. For `"ignore"`, `covariate.levels` is the natural level order, so the same expression works.
- `is.ordered[j] == FALSE` (`"partition"`): `splitval` is a comma-separated list of level **indices that go RIGHT**. Left is the complement, `!(x %in% covariate.levels[[j]][idx])`. Reading them as left gives max abs diff 3.900624; complementing gives 0.

Tests should cover all three modes plus an ordered factor, against both `predict()$predictions` and a probability forest.

title: randomForest categorical splits are read as numeric thresholds
description:
For a factor predictor, `randomForest::getTree()` returns a `split point` that is an integer whose **bits** name the levels going left, flagged by `model$forest$ncat[j] > 1`. `R/model-rf.R:52-58` sets `is_categorical = FALSE` and takes the value verbatim, and `R/model-rf.R:138` then emits `expr(!!col_sym <= !!split_val)`. Against a factor column that produces `f <= 11`, which warns `'<=' not meaningful for factors` and returns garbage.

```
RF y ~ x1 + f (4-level factor, ntree=5): max abs diff vs predict() = 6.121314
RF y ~ x1 + o (ordered factor, ntree=5): max abs diff              = 3.958060
.extract_rf_classprob with a factor:     max class-probability error = 1.0  (0 vs 1)
```

Bit decoding confirmed: `split point = 10` on `levels = a,b,c,d` means left = `{b, d}`; `= 11` means left = `{a, b, d}`.

**Fix.** In both `rf_tree_info_full()` and `build_nested_rf_tree()`, read `nc <- model$forest$ncat[var_idx]` and, when `nc > 1`, emit a categorical split with

```r
vals <- levels(x)[as.integer(intToBits(split_point))[1:nc] == 1]
```

A prototype of exactly this gave **max abs diff 0** on the 5-tree factor forest.

Add a test with a 4-level unordered factor and one with an ordered factor, comparing against `randomForest::predict()` for both the response and `type = "prob"`.

title: aorsf: a missing predictor returns a confident value where predict() refuses
description:
`aorsf::orsf()` declines to predict when new data contains a missing value. tidypredict returns a number instead, and the same number for every affected row:

```r
set.seed(1)
n <- 200
d <- data.frame(x = rnorm(n), z = rnorm(n))
d$y <- rnorm(n) + 2 * d$x - d$z
dna <- d
dna$x[1:5] <- NA

model <- aorsf::orsf(d, y ~ x + z, n_tree = 5)

predict(model, new_data = dna)
#> Error: Please remove missing values from new data, or impute them.

rlang::eval_tidy(tidypredict_fit(model), dna)[1:5]
#> 4.5231 4.5231 4.5231 4.5231 4.5231
```

aorsf splits on linear combinations of predictors, so a missing value makes the combination `NA`, the split condition `NA`, and `case_when()` sends the row to `.default` — the same mechanism as #294, but here the reference implementation refuses outright rather than routing the row somewhere.

The repeated value is the giveaway: all five rows take the identical `.default` path through every tree and land in the same leaf, regardless of what their other predictors say.

Expected behaviour is `NA` for those rows. The agreed policy is that tidypredict returns one value per input row and never drops rows, so where a backend cannot route a missing value the row should come back `NA` rather than a confident number.

This is distinct from #294, which is about backends that *do* route `NA` (rpart surrogates, LightGBM's `missing_type`) and route it differently from tidypredict. Filing separately since the fix here is "produce `NA`" rather than "reproduce the routing".

Found by sweeping missing-value handling across every supported class.

title: `tidypredict_test()`: `max_rows`, zero-row and all-NA handling
description:
Four independent faults in the test helper and its reporter.

- [ ] **`xgb_booster()` heads `df` but not `xg_df`, so `max_rows` always errors.** `R/tidypredict_test.R:277-279`:
  ```r
  tidypredict_test(m, as.data.frame(x), xg_df = d, max_rows = 5)
  #> Error in data.frame(...): arguments imply differing number of rows: 32, 5
  ```
  Fix: subset `xg_df` alongside `df`, via `xgboost::slice()` for a DMatrix.

- [ ] **`max_rows` greater than `nrow()` fabricates NA rows for LightGBM and CatBoost.** `:332-334` and `:418-420` use `head(df, max_rows)` (which caps) for the data frame but `lgb_df[seq_len(max_rows), , drop = FALSE]` (which pads with `NA`) for the matrix, giving either a length mismatch or NA predictions. Fix: `seq_len(min(max_rows, nrow(lgb_df)))`.

- [ ] **All-`NA` predictions crash the reporter with a base-R error.** `R/test-results.R:89-92`: `alert <- any(counts > 0)` is `NA` when any difference is `NA`, so `if (!alert)` throws "missing value where TRUE/FALSE needed". Same at `:146-150` (`test_results_class()`) and `:175-177` (multiclass). Fix: `sum(..., na.rm = TRUE)` plus an explicit count of NA rows reported in the message — silently dropping them would be worse.

- [ ] **Zero-row input reports a spurious pass plus a `-Inf` warning.** `R/test-results.R:70-71`: `max(abs(numeric(0)))` warns "no non-missing arguments to max; returning -Inf", and the message then claims "All results are within the difference threshold". Reproduced with `tidypredict_test(lm(...), df = mtcars[0, ])` and with `max_rows = 0`. Fix: short-circuit on `nrow(raw_results) == 0` with a distinct message.

Also worth addressing: two `tidypredict_test()` defaults cannot work. The C5.0 method defaults `df = NULL` and `predict(model, NULL)` errors with "newdata must be non-null" (`:103-113`); `tidypredict_test.rpart` (`R/model-rpart.R:210`) defaults to `df = model$model`, which is `NULL` unless the user fitted with `model = TRUE`, so it dies in `predict.rpart` with "object 'wt' not found". Both should check for a missing `df` and abort with an actionable message.

Finally, the default `threshold = 1e-12` flags correct float32 models — a correct 5-round xgboost model reports "Fitted records above the threshold: 32, Max difference: 3.35e-06". Consider a looser default for float32 boosters, or at least a note in `?tidypredict_test`.

title: `dbplyr` is in Suggests but used unconditionally
description:
`R/to_sql.R:14-16` and `:33-35` call `dbplyr::translate_sql()` with no `rlang::check_installed("dbplyr")` guard, and the `@examples` at `:8` and `:27` call `library(dbplyr)` / `simulate_dbi()` unguarded. CRAN flags unconditional use of a Suggests-only package in examples.

**Fix.** Add `rlang::check_installed("dbplyr")` at the top of both functions, and wrap the examples in `@examplesIf rlang::is_installed("dbplyr")`.

Related: `tidypredict_sql()` and `tidypredict_sql_interval()` are exported, advertised in the README function table and given `@examples`, yet marked `@keywords internal` at `:12` and `:31`, which hides them from the pkgdown reference index and flags them as internal in the help index. These are core user-facing functions; the tag should go.

title: `tidypredict_interval()` returns `numeric(0)` for every `glm`
description:
`R/model-lm.R:96-98` sets `sigma2` only when `length(summary(model)$sigma^2) > 0`. `summary.glm()` has no `$sigma` element, so `NULL^2` has length 0 and `pm$general$sigma2` is never set for a glm. `te_interval_glm()` (`R/model-glm.R:16-30`) then splices `NULL` straight into the expression:

```r
g <- glm(mpg ~ wt, data = mtcars)
tidypredict_interval(g)
#> 2.042 * sqrt((-0.1767) * (-0.1767) * NULL + ... + NULL)
rlang::eval_tidy(tidypredict_interval(g), mtcars)   # numeric(0)
tidypredict_to_column(mtcars, g, add_interval = TRUE)
#> Error: `upper` must be size 32 or 1, not 0.
```

No error, no warning, zero rows out. **The existing test only asserts `expect_type(interval, "language")`** (`test-model-glm.R:106-110`), so it passes.

**Fix.** Use the dispersion for glm:

```r
pm$general$sigma2 <- if (inherits(model, "glm")) {
  summary(model)$dispersion
} else {
  summary(model)$sigma^2
}
```

Verified equivalent: `summary(glm(mpg~wt+disp, data=mtcars))$dispersion == summary(lm(mpg~wt+disp, mtcars))$sigma^2` (both 8.506293). With that substitution `fit ± interval` reproduces `predict.lm(interval = "prediction")` to 1e-14.

Please replace the `expect_type()` assertion with a numeric comparison against `predict(lm_equivalent, interval = "prediction")` — the weak assertion is the reason this went unnoticed.

title: catboost: float borders are compared as doubles
description:
catboost borders are exactly representable floats (e.g. `-2.6778302192687988`) and catboost compares them in float32, so a value one part in 1e9 above a border still bins left. Probing all 49 borders of one feature, **49/49 rows at `border + 1e-9` disagreed with `catboost.predict()`, by up to 0.828 absolute**.

**Fix.** Apply `f32_split_boundary(split$border, "upper")` at `R/model-catboost.R:531` and `:588`, matching what Cubist and xgboost already do.

Two smaller items in the same file, fine to fold in:

- Multiclass bias is truncated to its first element (`:121` takes `scale_and_bias[[2]][[1]]`, then `apply_catboost_scale_bias()` applies that one value to every class score). catboost stores one bias per approx dimension (`[1,[0,0,0]]` observed). Harmless today because multiclass bias is always 0 (`boost_from_average` is unavailable there), but wrong by construction.
- Two silent degradations that should abort instead of guessing: `:53-56` reads the objective only when `loss_function` is a list with `$type`, otherwise `build_fit_formula_catboost_nested()` (`:811`) defaults to `"RMSE"` — which would drop the sigmoid from a Logloss model; and `:61-70` yields `num_class = 1` for a multiclass objective lacking `class_params$class_names`, silently summing all per-class trees into one expression.
- Doc nit: the `get_catboost_missing()` comment at `:663-666` inverts the branch names ("AsTrue: NaN goes left (where condition > border is TRUE)"); in this file `"more"` is the *right* branch. The code is correct.

Separately, **CTR / target-statistic splits give a cryptic internal error** and deserve a proper guard: with catboost's default `one_hot_max_size`, a categorical feature becomes an `OnlineCtr` split, and `get_catboost_tree()` (`:581-592`) plus `make_float_split()` (`:521`) treat any non-`OneHotFeature` split as a float split, so `split$float_feature_index` is `NULL` and it dies with "attempt to select less than one element in get1index". Add an explicit `split_type` allowlist with an abort naming CTR features and suggesting `one_hot_max_size`.

title: The documented YAML save workflow truncates thresholds to 7 digits
description:
`vignettes/save.Rmd:49,61` recommends `yaml::write_yaml(parsed, file)`. yaml's default numeric format is `%.7g`, so a split threshold of `0.16793434299541318` reloads as `0.1679343` and rows sitting between the two values change branch:

```
ctree(y ~ x1 + f), parse -> write_yaml -> as_parsed_model:
  5/200 rows differ, max abs diff = 1.076529
cforest, same round trip:
  max abs diff = 0.5924153
```

Every tree parser is affected (rpart 4.7e-08, rf/ranger 3.5e-08 on the fits tested — the same defect, just with no tie flipped on that data). The existing aorsf test papers over it with `tolerance = 1e-6` (`test-model-aorsf.R:89`), which is a symptom rather than a fix.

**Fix.** Recommend and use `yaml::write_yaml(x, file, precision = 17)` in `vignettes/save.Rmd` and in the tests. Consider whether tidypredict should provide a thin save helper that sets this correctly, so users cannot get it wrong.

title: `rank()` used as an array index picks the wrong factor variable
description:
`R/model-lm.R:171`:

```r
sole_cat_match <- cat_match_vars[rank(-nchar(cat_match_vars))][[1]]
```

Ranks are used as positions. With three or more candidate names that are prefixes of one another, the intended "longest match" is wrong:

```r
df <- data.frame(y = rnorm(30), x = rnorm(30),
                 xyz = factor(rep(c("A","B","C"), each = 10)), xy = rnorm(30))
tidypredict_fit(lm(y ~ x + xyz + xy, df))
#> ... (ifelse(xy == "zB", 1, 0) * 0.1261) + (ifelse(xy == "zC", 1, 0) * -0.2623) ...
```

Candidates `c("x","xyz","xy")` have `nchar` `(1,3,2)`, so `rank(-nchar)` is `(3,1,2)` and `"xy"` is selected instead of `"xyz"`. **Max abs diff 0.2623**, silently, with no error or warning.

This is in `parse_label_lm()`, so it affects **lm, glm, rq, multinom, nnet and earth**.

**Fix.**

```r
sole_cat_match <- cat_match_vars[[which.max(nchar(cat_match_vars))]]
```

Test with three predictors whose names are nested prefixes, at least one of them a factor.

title: Earth: Add support for additional GLM link functions (probit, cloglog)
description:
## Description

When using `earth::earth()` with GLM, some link functions are not supported by `tidypredict_fit()`.

## Currently Unsupported Links

| Family | Link | Status |
|--------|------|--------|
| `binomial` | probit | ❌ Unsupported |
| `binomial` | cloglog | ❌ Unsupported |

## Current Error

```r
library(earth)
library(tidypredict)

model <- earth(
  survived ~ age + sibsp,
  data = earth::etitanic,
  glm = list(family = binomial(link = "probit"))
)

tidypredict_fit(model)
#> Error: Combination of family and link are not supported.
```

## Link Function Formulas

For reference, the inverse link functions are:

- **probit**: `pnorm(eta)` (normal CDF)
- **cloglog**: `1 - exp(-exp(eta))` (complementary log-log)

## Files to Modify

- `R/te-compile.R` - Add link function implementations

title: LightGBM linear trees not supported
description:
When using LightGBM's linear trees (`linear_tree=TRUE`), `tidypredict_fit()` produces incorrect predictions. Linear trees add linear regression models within each leaf node, but tidypredict only extracts the constant leaf values, not the linear coefficients.

## Reprex

```r
library(lightgbm)
library(tidypredict)

set.seed(123)
X <- data.matrix(mtcars[, c("mpg", "cyl", "disp")])
y <- mtcars$hp

# Must set linear_tree in Dataset params
dtrain <- lgb.Dataset(
  X, label = y, 
  colnames = c("mpg", "cyl", "disp"),
  params = list(linear_tree = TRUE)
)

model <- lgb.train(
  params = list(
    num_leaves = 4L,
    learning_rate = 0.5,
    objective = "regression",
    min_data_in_leaf = 1L,
    linear_tree = TRUE
  ),
  data = dtrain,
  nrounds = 5L,
  verbose = -1L
)

fit <- tidypredict_fit(model)
native <- predict(model, X)
tidy <- rlang::eval_tidy(fit, as.data.frame(X))

max(abs(tidy - native))
#> [1] 19.32875
```

## Notes

This is a complex feature to implement as it would require:
1. Extracting linear coefficients from the model JSON dump
2. Building formulas that include both the tree structure and linear models within leaves

May be better to document as unsupported and throw a clear error message rather than implement.

title: CatBoost: Add support for additional objectives (Huber, LogCosh, Expectile, Tweedie)
description:
## Description

Several CatBoost objectives are not currently supported by `tidypredict_fit()`.

## Objectives to Add

| Objective | Transformation | Implementation |
|-----------|---------------|----------------|
| `Huber` | identity | Add to `catboost_identity_objectives` |
| `LogCosh` | identity | Add to `catboost_identity_objectives` |
| `Expectile` | identity | Add to `catboost_identity_objectives` |
| `Tweedie` | exp | Needs special handling (log-link) |

## Current Error

```r
library(catboost)
library(tidypredict)

set.seed(123)
X <- data.matrix(mtcars[, c("mpg", "cyl", "disp")])
y <- mtcars$hp

pool <- catboost.load_pool(
  X,
  label = y,
  feature_names = as.list(c("mpg", "cyl", "disp"))
)

model <- catboost.train(
  pool,
  params = list(
    iterations = 5L,
    depth = 3L,
    learning_rate = 0.5,
    loss_function = "Huber:delta=1.0",
    logging_level = "Silent",
    allow_writing_files = FALSE
  )
)

# Error: Unsupported objective: "Huber".
# ℹ Supported objectives: "RMSE", "MAE", "Quantile", "MAPE", "Poisson", 
#   "Logloss", "CrossEntropy", "MultiClass", and "MultiClassOneVsAll".
tidypredict_fit(model)
```

## Notes

- Huber, LogCosh, and Expectile use identity transformation (like MAE) - simple to add
- Tweedie uses log-link (predictions on log scale need exp() transformation)

title: glmnet: add support for cox family
description:
## Description

Add support for `glmnet` models trained with `family = "cox"` for Cox proportional hazards regression.

## Current Behavior

```r
library(glmnet)
library(tidypredict)
library(survival)

x <- as.matrix(mtcars[, -c(1, 8)])
y <- Surv(mtcars$mpg, mtcars$vs)

model <- glmnet(x, y, family = "cox", lambda = 0.5)
tidypredict_fit(model)
#> Error: Model fit with this `family` is not supported.
```

## Expected Behavior

Should return a formula for the linear predictor (log hazard ratio).

## Notes

Cox models produce a `coxnet` class. The linear predictor can be converted to a formula similar to other GLM families.

title: Fix LightGBM RF boosting predictions
description:
When using LightGBM's Random Forest boosting (`boosting="rf"`), `tidypredict_fit()` produces incorrect predictions. The predictions are `nrounds` times too large because RF averages trees while tidypredict sums them.

## Reprex

```r
library(lightgbm)
library(tidypredict)

set.seed(123)
X <- data.matrix(mtcars[, c("mpg", "cyl", "disp")])
y <- mtcars$hp
dtrain <- lgb.Dataset(X, label = y, colnames = c("mpg", "cyl", "disp"))

model <- lgb.train(
  params = list(
    boosting = "rf",
    num_leaves = 4L,
    objective = "regression",
    min_data_in_leaf = 1L,
    bagging_freq = 1,
    bagging_fraction = 0.8
  ),
  data = dtrain,
  nrounds = 5L,
  verbose = -1L
)

fit <- tidypredict_fit(model)
native <- predict(model, X)
tidy <- rlang::eval_tidy(fit, as.data.frame(X))

head(data.frame(native = native, tidy = tidy, ratio = tidy / native))
#>     native     tidy ratio
#> 1 103.5594 517.7968     5
#> 2 103.5594 517.7968     5
#> 3  95.7455 478.7274     5
#> 4 103.5594 517.7968     5
#> 5 191.0838 955.4190     5
#> 6 103.5594 517.7968     5

# Dividing by nrounds fixes it
max(abs(tidy / 5 - native))
#> [1] 0
```

## Fix

In `build_fit_formula_lgb()` or `build_lgb_tree_sum()`, divide the tree sum by `nrounds` when `boosting="rf"`.

title: CatBoost: Non-oblivious trees (Depthwise/Lossguide grow_policy) not supported
description:
## Description

When using `grow_policy="Depthwise"` or `grow_policy="Lossguide"` with CatBoost, `tidypredict_fit()` fails with "Model has no trees" error.

## Root Cause

CatBoost stores trees differently depending on the grow policy:
- `SymmetricTree` (default): Trees in `oblivious_trees` JSON field
- `Depthwise` / `Lossguide`: Trees in `trees` JSON field (non-oblivious)

The current parser only handles `oblivious_trees`.

## Reprex

```r
library(catboost)
library(tidypredict)

set.seed(123)
X <- data.matrix(mtcars[, c("mpg", "cyl", "disp")])
y <- mtcars$hp

pool <- catboost.load_pool(
  X,
  label = y,
  feature_names = as.list(c("mpg", "cyl", "disp"))
)

model <- catboost.train(
  pool,
  params = list(
    iterations = 5L,
    depth = 3L,
    learning_rate = 0.5,
    loss_function = "RMSE",
    grow_policy = "Depthwise",  # or "Lossguide"
    logging_level = "Silent",
    allow_writing_files = FALSE
  )
)

# Error: Model has no trees.
tidypredict_fit(model)
```

## Suggested Fix

Either:
1. Add support for parsing non-oblivious trees from the `trees` JSON field
2. Document as unsupported with a clear error message explaining why

title: Ranger: Predictions are num.trees × too large (sums instead of averages)
description:
## Description

Random forests average tree predictions, but `tidypredict_fit()` sums them. This causes predictions to be `num.trees` × too large.

## Reprex

```r
library(ranger)
library(tidypredict)
library(dplyr)

set.seed(123)
model <- ranger(
  mpg ~ cyl + disp + hp,
  data = mtcars,
  num.trees = 5,
  max.depth = 3,
  seed = 123,
  num.threads = 2
)

native <- predict(model, mtcars)$predictions
fit <- tidypredict_fit(model)
tidy <- rlang::eval_tidy(fit, mtcars)

# Tidy predictions are 5x native (num.trees = 5)
head(data.frame(native = native, tidy = tidy, ratio = tidy/native))
#>     native      tidy ratio
#> 1 20.70950 103.54750     5
#> 2 20.70950 103.54750     5
#> 3 24.44381 118.73155     5
#> 4 19.40033  97.00167     5
#> 5 16.26683  81.33417     5
#> 6 19.40033  97.00167     5
```

## Suggested Fix

In `tidypredict_fit.ranger()`, divide the result by `model$num.trees`:

```r
tidypredict_fit.ranger <- function(model) {
parsedmodel <- parse_model(model)
  res <- generate_case_when_trees(parsedmodel)
  tree_sum <- reduce_addition(res)
  # Divide by number of trees to get average
expr(!!tree_sum / !!model$num.trees)
}
```

Note: The `num.trees` value should be stored in the parsed model during `parse_model.ranger()` so it's available when using a saved/loaded parsed model.

title: partykit: stump trees (no splits) cause error

title: randomForest: Split operator uses < instead of <= for left child
description:
## Description

`tidypredict_fit()` for randomForest models uses the wrong comparison operator for tree splits. randomForest uses `<=` (less or equal) for the left child, but tidypredict uses `<` (less than).

Same bug as ranger (#189).

## Impact

When a data point has a value exactly equal to a split value, it goes to the wrong child node, causing incorrect predictions.

## Reprex

```r
library(randomForest)
library(tidypredict)
library(dplyr)

set.seed(42)
df <- data.frame(x = c(1, 2, 3, 4), y = c(10, 20, 100, 200))
model <- randomForest(y ~ x, data = df, ntree = 1, nodesize = 2, maxnodes = 3)

# Tree has split at x=3
tree <- randomForest::getTree(model, 1)
print(tree)
#>   left daughter right daughter split var split point status prediction
#> 1             2              3         1           3     -3        155
#> 2             0              0         0           0     -1         20
#> 3             0              0         0           0     -1        200

test_df <- data.frame(x = c(2.99, 3, 3.01))

native <- predict(model, test_df)
#> [1]  20  20 200  (x=3 goes LEFT with <=)

fit <- tidypredict_fit(model)
# case_when(x < 3 ~ 20, .default = 200)/1L

tidy <- rlang::eval_tidy(fit, test_df)
#> [1]  20 200 200  (x=3 goes RIGHT with <)

# BUG: x=3 gives different results
native[2]  # 20 (correct - uses x <= 3)
tidy[2]    # 200 (wrong - uses x < 3)
```

## Suggested Fix

In `R/model-rf.R`, `parse_rf_path()` function:
- Change `op <- "less"` → `op <- "less-equal"` for left child
- Change `op <- "more-equal"` → `op <- "more"` for right child

title: glmnet: family function syntax not supported
description:
## Description

When using family function syntax (`gaussian()`, `binomial()`, `poisson()`) instead of string syntax (`"gaussian"`, `"binomial"`, `"poisson"`), `tidypredict_fit()` fails with "Model fit with this `family` is not supported."

## Reprex

```r
library(glmnet)
library(tidypredict)

x <- as.matrix(mtcars[, -1])
y <- mtcars$mpg

# String syntax works
model_str <- glmnet(x, y, family = "gaussian", lambda = 0.5)
tidypredict_fit(model_str)  # Works

# Function syntax fails
model_func <- glmnet(x, y, family = gaussian(), lambda = 0.5)
tidypredict_fit(model_func)
#> Error: Model fit with this `family` is not supported.
```

Same issue with `binomial()` and `poisson()`.

## Root Cause

Models created with function syntax have class `glmnetfit, glmnet` instead of `elnet, glmnet` (or `lognet`/`fishnet`). The code at `R/model-glmnet.R:53-66` only checks for `elnet`, `lognet`, and `fishnet` classes.

## Suggested Fix

Add handling for `glmnetfit` class by checking `model$family$family` and `model$family$link`:

```r
} else if (inherits(model, "glmnetfit")) {

  pm$general$family <- model$family$family
  pm$general$link <- model$family$link
}
```

title: glm: family function syntax triggers false error
description:
## Description

When using family function syntax (`gaussian()`, `binomial()`, `poisson()`) instead of string syntax (`"gaussian"`, `"binomial"`, `"poisson"`), `tidypredict_fit()` incorrectly detects the family function as a "function inside the formula" and errors.

## Reprex

```r
library(tidypredict)

# String syntax works
model_str <- glm(mpg ~ wt + hp, data = mtcars, family = "gaussian")
tidypredict_fit(model_str)  # Works

# Function syntax fails
model_func <- glm(mpg ~ wt + hp, data = mtcars, family = gaussian())
tidypredict_fit(model_func)
#> Error: Functions inside the formula are not supported.
#> ℹ Functions detected: "gaussian".
```

## Impact

This bug also prevents using non-default link functions, since they require function syntax:

```r
# These all fail:
glm(..., family = binomial(link = "probit"))
glm(..., family = binomial(link = "cloglog"))
glm(..., family = poisson(link = "sqrt"))
glm(..., family = gaussian(link = "log"))
```

## Root Cause

The function detection logic checks the entire model call, not just the formula. The `gaussian()`, `binomial()`, etc. functions in `model$call` trigger the error.

## Suggested Fix

Modify the function detection to only check the formula, not the family argument in the call.

title: consider that xgboost converts data to 32 bit float internally
description:
Hi @edgararuiz, I'm the author of the [article](https://rviews.rstudio.com/2018/11/07/in-database-xgboost-predictions-with-r/) mentioned by @JiaxiangBU in this [issue](https://github.com/tidymodels/tidypredict/issues/40).  I wanted to mention the following in case if helps with development:

I discovered after writing the article was that xgboost converts data internally to 32-bit floats, and the resulting coefficients in the `xgb.dump` JSON correspond to this treatment.  This might lead to errors, particularly with logistic regression objective functions.  See the discussions at: https://github.com/dmlc/xgboost/issues/4097

In other words, applying the coefficients as-is would assume the data in the database is represented as 32-bit floats.  A good test would be to run xgboost predictions using the model binary (loaded via xgb.load) and then compare them with the tidypredict SQL results produced on the same data stored in a database, particularly for logistic regression objective functions.

I hope this is helpful!

title: [Feature Request] case statements needed for grouped regression
description:
I use grouped regressions often (aka [Many Models](http://r4ds.had.co.nz/many-models.html)). Though your package makes it mostly painless to create grouped model sql code, maybe it would be nice to have a convenience function to do this.

Hopefully the code below illustrates what I am thinking. 

```r
# load libs
library(tidyverse)
library(tidypredict)
library(gapminder)

# make model function
country_model <- function(df) {
  lm(lifeExp ~ year, data = df)
}

# nest data for grouped regression
by_country <- gapminder %>% 
  group_by(country, continent) %>% 
  nest() %>% 
  mutate(model = map(data, country_model)) %>% 
  # use tidypredict to make sql strings by model
  mutate(sql_txt = map(model,~tidypredict_sql(., dbplyr::simulate_mssql()))) %>% 
  # add some case statements -- more work needed here
  mutate(case_string = paste0("WHEN COUNTRY = ", "'", country, "'", " THEN ")) %>% 
  # paste case statements to model sql
  mutate(full_string = paste0(case_string, sql_txt))
  
# paste all of the models together with case statements and return one big glob
# of text for sql
by_country %>% 
  unnest(full_string) %>% 
  summarise(full_sql_text = toString(full_string)) %>% 
  as.list()
```

The first few entries are shown below. I am sure there are many ways to implement this in a cleaner fashion than what I did.

```r
WHEN COUNTRY = 'Afghanistan' THEN -507.534271561773 + (`year`) * (0.275328671328672), 
WHEN COUNTRY = 'Albania' THEN -594.072510955711 + (`year`) * (0.334683216783217),
WHEN COUNTRY = 'Algeria' THEN -1067.85903962704 + (`year`) * (0.569279720279723)
...
```

Would it be possible to add some convenience function to do some lifting for building case statements needed for grouped regression?

title: Binomial MARS model returns Gaussian coefficients when parsed in tidypredict_fit() and tidypredict_sql()
description:
It appears that tidypredict_fit() and tidypredict_sql() are returned a parsed model that has the Gaussian coefficients instead of the Binomial coefficients when a MARS model is fit using the earth package. The example below was done using R version 4.0.2, tidypredict_0.4.8 and earth_5.3.0. A comparison to parsed models using glm() is also included for reference. 
```{r setup}
library(earth)
library(tidyverse)
library(tidypredict)
data("etitanic", package = "earth")
```
# MARS w/ Binomial

```{r MARSMod1}
mars.mod.1 <- 
  earth(
    survived ~ age + sex,
    data = etitanic,
    glm = list(family = binomial)
  )
coef(mars.mod.1)
#> (Intercept)     sexmale    h(9-age) 
#>   1.0499562  -2.4754699   0.1692326
```

# MARS w/ Gaussian

```{r MARSMod2}
mars.mod.2 <-
  earth(
    survived ~ age + sex,
    data = etitanic,
    glm = list(family = gaussian)
  )
coef(mars.mod.2)
#> (Intercept)     sexmale    h(9-age) 
#>  0.73782144 -0.54239536  0.02975461
```

The parsed model w/ binomial returns the Gaussian model coefficients with the Sigmoid function applied

```{r MARSTidyPred1}
tidypredict_fit(mars.mod.1)
#> 1 - 1/(1 + exp(0.737821439264803 + (ifelse(age < 9, 9 - age, 
#>     0) * 0.0297546135084789) + (ifelse(sex == "male", 1, 0) * 
#>     -0.542395361228247)))
```

```{r MARSTidyPred2}
tidypredict_fit(mars.mod.2)
#> 0.737821439264803 + (ifelse(age < 9, 9 - age, 0) * 0.0297546135084789) + 
#>     (ifelse(sex == "male", 1, 0) * -0.542395361228247)
```

Compare tidypredict with predict (fit and pred columns are not the same)

```{r MARSPred}
etitanic %>%
  tidypredict_to_column(mars.mod.1) %>%
  mutate(pred = predict(mars.mod.1, type = "response")[,1]) %>%
  head(10) 

#>    pclass survived    sex     age sibsp parch       fit      pred
#> 1     1st        1 female 29.0000     0     0 0.6765193 0.7407665
#> 2     1st        1   male  0.9167     1     2 0.6072916 0.4856151
#> 3     1st        0 female  2.0000     1     2 0.7203309 0.9033125
#> 4     1st        0   male 30.0000     1     2 0.5487016 0.1937987
#> 5     1st        0 female 25.0000     1     2 0.6765193 0.7407665
#> 6     1st        1   male 48.0000     0     0 0.5487016 0.1937987
#> 7     1st        1 female 63.0000     1     0 0.6765193 0.7407665
#> 8     1st        0   male 39.0000     0     0 0.5487016 0.1937987
#> 9     1st        1 female 53.0000     2     0 0.6765193 0.7407665
#> 10    1st        0   male 71.0000     0     0 0.5487016 0.1937987
```

# Contrast with GLM

## GLM w/ binomial

```{r GLMMod1}
glm.mod.1 <-
  glm(
    survived ~ age + sex,
    data = etitanic,
    family = binomial
  )
coef(glm.mod.1)
#>  (Intercept)          age      sexmale 
#>  1.235414162 -0.004254246 -2.460689180
```

## GLM w/ Gaussian

```{r GLMMod2}
glm.mod.2 <-
  glm(
    survived ~ age + sex,
```

title: `lm()` doesn't like it when you can't invert the QR matrix
description:
Simple example here. Gets annoyed during `parse_model()`. I wonder if we can rewrite this model in orbital to avoid parsing.

```r
library(tidymodels)
library(orbital)

rec_spec <- recipe(Sale_Price ~ ., data = ames) |>
  step_nzv(all_numeric_predictors()) |>
  step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors()) |>
  step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors()) |>
  step_nzv(all_predictors())

mod_spec <- linear_reg()

wf_spec <- workflow(rec_spec, mod_spec)

wf_fit <- fit(wf_spec, ames)

orb <- orbital(wf_fit)
#> Error in qr.solve(qr.R(model$qr)): singular matrix 'a' in solve
```

Can get working model with:

``` r
library(tidymodels)
library(orbital)

rec_spec <- recipe(Sale_Price ~ ., data = ames) |>
  step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors()) |>
  step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors()) |>
  step_zv(all_predictors()) |>
  step_corr(all_predictors())

mod_spec <- linear_reg()

wf_spec <- workflow(rec_spec, mod_spec)

wf_fit <- fit(wf_spec, ames)

orb <- orbital(wf_fit)
```

title: Log links?
description:
Since I'm having such success with this so far:

In `te_fit_glm` you could support the log link (the most important one not already supported) with

```
  if ( link == "log") {
    assigned <- 1
    fit <- expr(exp(!! fit))
  }
```

Also, for the identity link it isn't necessary to check that you have `family=gaussian()`. The predictions will still work for any other family -- it's just intervals that don't, and you have a test for that in `te_interval_glm`

In fact, even for the logit link it's worth allowing family=quasibinomial, for modelling proportions between 0 and 1 that aren't probabilities, such as tip as a %age of payment in the big NYC taxi dataset.

title: [Feature request] Add support for decision tree from the rpart package
description:
Classification And Regression Tree (CART) is a very popular model so I think it should be included in the supported model list of `tidypredict`.

At first it seems that an `rpart` model can be obtained by training a `randomForest` model with `ntrees`=1 and `mtry`=<number_of_predictors>; however, there is no way to prune the tree using cost-complexity pruning.

Even though in most cases, `rpart` is inferior to `randomForest` in terms of accuracy, there are still some circumstances (e.g., when the data set is big, or when the relationship between predictors and outcome is straightforward) where `rpart` is preferred.

title: Feature Request: Add support for in-database goodness-of-fit computations
description: For example, if I pull down a sample of data, run a `glm`, it'd be awesome to be able to use the entire rest of my data as the test set, using `tidypredict::tidypredict_to_column()` and some currently nonexistent functionality to run AUC or R^2 on remaining data.

title: [Feature request] approximate prediction using lookup table for gam and other models not returning explicit rules.
description: Accommodation for models that do not produce explicit rules intercepts and slopes like for mcgv::gam models by using a lookup table to generate approximate prediction. Example: https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/mgcv/html/predict.gam.html and https://stats.stackexchange.com/questions/406566/using-gam-outside-statistical-modelling-software-in-datatabase-outside-r

title: [Feature request] returning rules that can easily be used in other languages (VBA, Excel formula)
description: Output of a syntax easily adaptable by power Excel/VBA/C users.
